lessons.title: What Ethics Is and Why Engineers Need It
lessons.content:
Imagine you are a young programmer at a food delivery company in Dhaka. One evening your manager says: 'Add a small piece of code that quietly reads every user's contact list. Marketing wants it. Nobody will notice.' The code is easy. Ten lines. You could finish it before dinner. But a small voice in your head asks: 'Should I?' That small voice is where this whole course begins. Knowing how to build something is a technical skill. Knowing whether you should build it, and what the law says about it, is what this course is about.

What this course is: Professional Ethics and Cyber Law has two halves that keep touching each other. Ethics asks 'What is the right thing to do?' Law asks 'What does society force me to do, and what happens if I don't?' Engineers need both. A doctor learns medicine and also medical ethics. A computer engineer learns programming and also what is fair, honest and legal when that programming touches real people.

Morals: Morals are the beliefs about right and wrong that a person or a community already holds. You probably learned many at home: don't lie, don't steal, help people in trouble, respect elders. Morals are often learned by habit and example, not by argument. Two families, or two countries, can have slightly different morals.

Ethics: Ethics is the careful, reasoned study of morals. Instead of saying 'this is wrong because my grandmother said so', ethics asks 'why is it wrong, and would the reason hold up if a smart person argued against it?' Ethics is like the mathematics of right and wrong. You state your reasons, you test them on examples, and you check that you are consistent. If you say stealing is wrong, ethics asks whether downloading a paid app for free is also stealing, and why or why not.

Law: Law is the set of rules a government writes down and enforces with courts, fines and prison. Law and ethics overlap a lot, but they are not the same thing. Some things are legal but unethical: for example, in a country with no privacy law, it may be legal to sell your users' phone numbers to advertisers, yet most people would call it a betrayal. Some things were illegal but ethical: people who broke unjust laws to protect others are often remembered as heroes. And law is usually slow. Technology arrives first and the law catches up years later.

Etiquette: Etiquette is simple good manners: not typing in ALL CAPITALS in a group chat, replying to emails politely, not taking calls loudly in the library. Breaking etiquette makes you rude, not evil. A useful habit is to put any question into the right box. Is this a manners question, an ethics question, or a legal question? Often it is more than one.

A quick worked sort: Let us put four actions into boxes. One: replying 'k' to your teacher's long email. That is etiquette. Two: copying a classmate's assignment. That is ethics, and also a university rule. Three: breaking into a bank's server. That is ethics and a crime under cyber law. Four: building an app that tracks the location of your users without telling them. That is clearly an ethics problem, and in many countries it is also illegal under data protection law. Sorting like this helps you know which tools to use.

A short history: Computer ethics is younger than computers, but not by much. In 1950 the mathematician Norbert Wiener, who founded the field of cybernetics, wrote a book called 'The Human Use of Human Beings'. He warned that automatic machines would change work, power and freedom, and that society should think about this early. In the mid-1970s Walter Maner started using the phrase 'computer ethics' for a university course, and in 1985 Deborah Johnson published one of the first textbooks with that title, the same year as Moor's paper. Since then, every new wave, from personal computers to the internet, smartphones, social media and AI, has brought new questions to the table.

Why computing makes ethics harder: Ethics is thousands of years old, so why does computer science need its own course? Because computers change four things. The first is scale. A shopkeeper who cheats cheats a few customers. A programmer who hides a cheating rule in an app used by 10 million people cheats 10 million people in one evening. The second is speed. A bad decision spreads at internet speed. The third is copying. A digital file can be copied perfectly, millions of times, at almost zero cost, which turns old ideas about stealing upside down. The fourth is invisibility. Users cannot see the code, so they must trust that the code does what it says.

Scale, worked with numbers: Suppose a payment app rounds every transaction down and keeps the leftover fraction of a taka. One transaction loses only 0.40 taka. That sounds like nothing. But if the app handles 5 million transactions a day, that is 0.40 times 5,000,000, which is 2,000,000 taka per day, and about 730 million taka in a year. A tiny unfair rule, multiplied by scale, becomes a huge harm. This is why engineers must think about small decisions very seriously.

The policy vacuum: The philosopher James Moor wrote a famous paper in 1985 called 'What Is Computer Ethics?'. His idea was simple. Computers let us do new things, and for those new things there are often no clear rules yet. He called this a policy vacuum. When cars were invented, there were no traffic rules. When social media arrived, there were no rules about deleting someone's photos or about fake news. In a policy vacuum, engineers often decide first, simply by writing the code. So engineers become rule makers whether they like it or not.

Who gets affected: In ethics we use the word stakeholder for anyone affected by a decision. For a food delivery app, stakeholders include customers, riders, restaurant owners, the company's investors, the programmers themselves, and even people who never use the app, like pedestrians on the road when riders are pushed to drive faster. A good engineer learns to list stakeholders before deciding, because the people who are not in the meeting room are often the ones who get hurt.

Why employers care: Companies want engineers they can trust with money, data and safety. A single data leak can destroy a company's reputation in a week. Banks, mobile financial services, hospitals and government projects in Bangladesh all handle sensitive data. They look for people who will say 'wait, this is risky' at the right moment. Ethics is not a soft extra. It is part of being employable.

Why the law cares: Governments around the world, including Bangladesh, have written cyber laws, copyright laws and data protection rules. Breaking them can mean fines, lawsuits or prison. Many young people get into trouble not because they are evil, but because they did not know the rules. 'I was just testing' or 'everyone downloads cracked software' is not a legal defence. Knowing the law protects you.

Is ethics just opinion? A common objection is: 'Right and wrong are just personal opinions, so why study them?' Notice that we do not treat all opinions as equal in other areas. If someone says 2 + 2 = 5, we show them why they are wrong. Ethics is not as exact as arithmetic, but reasons can still be strong or weak. 'It is fine to leak user passwords because I was bored' is a weak reason. 'We should delay the launch because the payment bug could take money from users' is a strong one. Ethics trains you to tell the difference, and to explain it to others calmly.

What ethics is not: Ethics is not about feeling guilty all the time, and it is not about religion only, though many people's ethics are shaped by their faith. It is not a list of things to memorise. It is a way of thinking: noticing a problem, asking who is affected, weighing options, and giving reasons that other people can check. Two good people can still disagree. The goal is not to win an argument but to reach a decision you can defend honestly.

The course map: We will move in five parts. First, ethical theories and a step-by-step decision method (lessons 02 to 04). Second, the professional side: what a profession is, codes of ethics, workplace dilemmas, software failures and academic honesty (05 to 09). Third, intellectual property and licences (10 to 12). Fourth, privacy and data protection (13 to 15). Fifth, computer crime and cyber law, including Bangladesh's laws, digital evidence and ethical hacking (16 to 21), then e-commerce, free speech, AI fairness and social impact (22 to 25).

Real-life example 1, the contact list: Back to our manager's request. Step 1, is reading contacts needed to deliver food? No. Step 2, would users agree if asked clearly? Most would not. Step 3, who gets hurt? Users, and also their friends whose numbers get copied without ever installing the app. Step 4, is it legal? Under many data protection laws, collecting data without a clear purpose and consent is not allowed. So the ethical choice is to push back, suggest an honest alternative such as an 'invite friends' button that the user presses, and write your concern down in an email. One quiet decision protects thousands of people.

Real-life example 2, the exam result portal: A university in Bangladesh asks a student team to build a result portal. To save time, a team member suggests showing results by roll number with no login, so anyone can type any roll number and see anyone's grades. Technically it works. Ethically it exposes students' private results to classmates, relatives and strangers. A small login step, or showing only the student's own result, fixes it. The lesson: many ethical problems are not dramatic crimes, just careless shortcuts.

Common mistakes: Students often think 'if it is legal, it is fine'. Law is the minimum, not the goal. Another mistake is thinking ethics is only about personal honesty, while forgetting that design choices, like default settings, are ethical choices too. A third mistake is assuming that because a manager ordered something, the responsibility belongs only to the manager. Professional codes say you keep your own responsibility. Exams often ask you to define ethics, morals and law, to explain how computing raises new ethical issues, and to describe what a policy vacuum is.

Recap: Morals are beliefs we already hold, ethics is reasoned thinking about them, law is what the state enforces, and etiquette is manners. Computers make ethical questions bigger because of scale, speed, perfect copying and invisible code. Moor called the gap between new technology and old rules a policy vacuum, and engineers often fill it with their code. In the next lesson we look at the first big family of ethical theories: judging actions by their consequences.
key_points: Morals are beliefs about right and wrong; ethics is the reasoned study of them; law is enforced by the state; etiquette is manners.
Legal and ethical are not the same: some legal acts are unethical, and the law is often slower than technology.
Computing makes ethics harder because of scale, speed, perfect copying and invisible code.
A tiny unfair rule times millions of users becomes a huge harm, so small design choices matter.
James Moor (1985) described a policy vacuum: new technology arrives before rules exist, so engineers end up making the rules.
A stakeholder is anyone affected by a decision, including people who never use your product.
Ethics is a way of reasoning that others can check, not a list to memorise.
lessons.tip: Keep a small notebook (or notes app) of every ethical dilemma you notice in apps you use this semester. Real examples make every later lesson easier to understand.
lessons.task: Write down 6 actions from your daily digital life (for example, forwarding a WhatsApp rumour, using a cracked game, replying rudely in a group). Sort each into etiquette, ethics, law, or more than one, and write one line explaining your choice.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes ethics?
options: Rules written by the government and enforced by courts
Careful, reasoned thinking about what is right and wrong
Whatever your manager tells you to do
quiz.explain: Ethics is the reasoned study of morals. Law is enforced by the state and etiquette is manners.

quiz.q: An app keeps 0.40 taka from each of 5,000,000 daily transactions. How much does it take per day?
quiz.explain: 0.40 x 5,000,000 = 2,000,000 taka per day, which shows how scale turns a tiny rule into a big harm.

quiz.q: What did James Moor call the situation where new technology arrives before rules exist?
quiz.explain: Moor's 1985 paper described a policy vacuum: no clear policies yet for new computer-enabled actions.

quiz.q: Which of these is legal in many places but still widely seen as unethical?
options: Selling users' data without telling them, in a country with no privacy law
quiz.explain: Where no privacy law exists it may be legal, yet it betrays users' trust. The others are crimes almost everywhere.

quiz.q: Who counts as a stakeholder of a food delivery app?
options: Anyone affected, including riders, restaurants and pedestrians
quiz.explain: A stakeholder is anyone affected by the decision, including people who never use the app.

lessons.title: Ethical Theories I: Relativism and Judging by Consequences
lessons.content:
Think about a cricket umpire. When a batsman is hit on the pad, the umpire does not decide 'out' or 'not out' by mood. He follows a theory: the LBW rule. The rule has parts (where the ball pitched, where it hit, would it hit the stumps), and two umpires using the same rule usually reach the same answer. Ethical theories are like that for right and wrong. They are organised ways of reasoning, so that two people can follow the same steps and explain how they reached an answer. In this lesson and the next we meet the main theories. None is perfect, but each one gives you a useful lens.

Why theories at all: Without a theory, ethical arguments become shouting matches: 'This is wrong!' 'No, it's fine!' A theory gives you a structure: what counts as a good reason, what facts you need, and how to compare options. Philosophers have tested these theories for centuries against hard cases, so they come with known strengths and known weak spots. Knowing the weak spots is just as useful as knowing the strengths.

The two simple views we must deal with first: Before the serious theories, there are two popular shortcuts that many people already believe. They are subjective relativism and cultural relativism. Most textbooks show why they do not work well as complete theories, and understanding why sharpens your thinking.

Subjective relativism: This view says each person decides what is right for themselves. 'If you think piracy is fine, it is fine for you. If I think it is wrong, it is wrong for me.' It sounds tolerant and friendly. But look at the problems. First, it makes moral disagreement meaningless: if you and I disagree, we are both right, so there is nothing to discuss. Second, it cannot criticise anyone: a person who believes stealing from bKash accounts is fine would be 'right for himself'. Third, it blurs the line between doing what you want and doing what is right. Ethics is supposed to sometimes tell us to do what we do not want to do.

Cultural relativism: This view says right and wrong are whatever a society's customs say. There is a true observation inside it: different cultures really do have different practices, and we should be humble before judging. But as a full theory it has problems. If a society once accepted slavery, cultural relativism must say slavery was right there and then. It also cannot explain moral progress: if right just means 'what my society accepts', reformers who changed society for the better were simply wrong at the time. And online, which culture's rules apply to a website used in Dhaka, Delhi and Dallas at once? The internet makes this view especially hard to use.

Divine command theory, briefly: Many people ground their ethics in religion: right is what God commands. For believers this is meaningful and deeply motivating, and most religions agree on many core values like honesty and not harming others. As a tool for a mixed professional team, though, it has a practical limit: colleagues may follow different faiths or none, and holy texts do not mention software licences or facial recognition. So in a workplace we need reasons that people of any background can check. This does not reject anyone's faith. It just means we also need shared, secular reasoning.

Consequentialism: Now the first serious family. Consequentialism says an action is right or wrong depending on its consequences, its results. Ask: what will happen if I do this, and what will happen if I don't? Pick the option with the best overall results. This is how many engineers already think: weigh costs and benefits, choose the design with the best outcome.

Utilitarianism: The most famous consequentialist theory is utilitarianism, developed by Jeremy Bentham (1748 to 1832) and John Stuart Mill (1806 to 1873). The core is the principle of utility, often summarised as: act so as to produce the greatest good for the greatest number. 'Good' here usually means happiness or well-being, and 'bad' means suffering. Bentham even suggested measuring pleasure by its intensity, duration, certainty and how many people it reaches. Mill added that some pleasures, like learning and friendship, are of higher quality than others.

How to apply it, step by step: Step 1, list every stakeholder. Step 2, list the options. Step 3, for each option, estimate the benefit or harm to each stakeholder, using a simple score. Step 4, add up the scores. Step 5, choose the option with the highest total. Scores are rough guesses, but writing them down forces you to notice people you would have forgotten.

A worked utility table: A Dhaka university must decide whether to install CCTV cameras with facial recognition in all classrooms to track attendance. Score each group from minus 10 (very harmful) to plus 10 (very helpful). Option A, install it. Teachers save time: plus 4 for 200 teachers, so 800. Administration saves cost: plus 6 for 20 staff, so 120. Students lose privacy and feel watched: minus 3 for 8,000 students, so minus 24,000. Total: 800 + 120 minus 24,000 = minus 23,080. Option B, keep a simple QR-code attendance app: teachers plus 2 times 200 = 400, administration plus 3 times 20 = 60, students minus 0.5 times 8,000 = minus 4,000. Total: minus 3,540. Option C, keep paper attendance: everyone 0, total 0. With these guesses, utilitarianism picks C, and B beats A by a lot. Notice how the large number of students dominates the result.

Expected value, the engineer's version: Engineers often use a cousin of the utility calculation called expected harm, which is probability times impact. Suppose a payment bug has a 1 in 1,000 chance per day of wrongly charging 50,000 users 200 taka each. The impact if it happens is 50,000 x 200 = 10,000,000 taka. The expected harm per day is 10,000,000 / 1,000 = 10,000 taka, or about 3,650,000 taka a year. If fixing the bug costs two engineers one week, the fix is clearly worth it. This is utilitarian thinking in a tool engineers already know, and it makes 'it probably won't happen' arguments much easier to test.

A caution about numbers: Numbers make an argument look scientific, but they are only as honest as the guesses inside them. Someone who wants a particular answer can quietly give their own side bigger scores. A good habit is to show your table to people from different stakeholder groups and ask, 'Would you score this the same way?' If the answer flips when reasonable people change a score a little, the decision is close, and other theories should be consulted too.

Act utilitarianism: Act utilitarianism applies the calculation to each single action. 'Will this particular lie, right now, make things better overall?' It is flexible, but it has a famous problem. Imagine a hospital where secretly taking the organs of one healthy visitor could save five patients. A pure act calculation might say five lives beat one. Almost everyone feels this is monstrous, which shows act utilitarianism can justify terrible acts when numbers look good.

Rule utilitarianism: Rule utilitarianism fixes much of this. Instead of judging single actions, it asks: which general rule, if everyone followed it, would produce the best results? A rule like 'doctors may secretly harvest patients' organs' would destroy all trust in hospitals and cause huge harm, so the rule is rejected. In computing: 'engineers may hide security flaws if it helps quarterly profits' would, if followed by everyone, make all software untrustworthy. So the rule fails. Rule utilitarianism is often closer to everyday moral sense.

Strengths of utilitarianism: It is practical and familiar: governments use cost-benefit analysis for roads, vaccines and budgets. It treats every person's happiness as counting equally: a rickshaw puller's well-being counts exactly as much as a minister's. It focuses on real results instead of good intentions that go nowhere. And it fits naturally with engineering, where we already measure trade-offs.

Weaknesses of utilitarianism: First, we can rarely predict all consequences, especially for new technology used by millions. Second, happiness is hard to measure and compare between people. Third, it can ignore justice: if harming a small minority makes a large majority slightly happier, the sum may say yes. Our CCTV table showed the reverse case, where the majority's harm decided it, but flip the numbers and a minority can be crushed. Fourth, it ignores where we draw the boundary: should we count future users, animals, people in other countries? Fifth, it can demand too much: almost any free time could be used to help someone more.

Ethical egoism, briefly: Another consequence-based view says each person should act only in their own long-term self-interest. It is honest about human motives, and it reminds us that self-interest is not automatically evil. But as a professional ethic it fails badly: an engineer acting only for personal gain would ship dangerous code whenever it paid. Professional codes, as we will see, put the public first.

Real-life example 1, the battery-saving update: A phone maker discovers that old batteries cause sudden shutdowns. Option 1: quietly slow down old phones so they don't shut off. Option 2: slow them down and clearly tell users, offering cheap battery replacement. Option 3: do nothing. A utilitarian table shows Option 2 gives the best total: users avoid shutdowns and keep control, and trust is protected. Option 1 looks good short-term but, when discovered, trust collapses, and lawsuits follow. In fact, similar quiet throttling by a major phone maker led to public anger and legal settlements around 2017 to 2020. Hidden consequences are still consequences.

Real-life example 2, a traffic app in Dhaka: A navigation app could send cars through narrow residential lanes in Mohammadpur to save drivers 4 minutes each. For 10,000 drivers that is 40,000 minutes saved per day. But the lanes fill with cars, children cannot play outside and residents breathe more smoke. A careful utilitarian counts both sides, not only the users who opened the app. This is a key lesson: utilitarianism is only as good as the list of people you remember to count.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students often confuse act and rule utilitarianism; remember act judges one action, rule judges a general policy. Another mistake is saying 'utilitarianism means majority wins'. It means the total good is highest, which can occasionally favour a few people who would be hugely affected. Many students also forget that relativism is usually presented in textbooks to be criticised, not recommended. Typical exam questions: 'Explain cultural relativism and give two objections', 'Distinguish act and rule utilitarianism with an example', 'Apply utilitarianism to a computing case'.

Recap: Subjective relativism makes ethics personal taste and cannot criticise anything; cultural relativism respects differences but cannot explain moral progress or work across the global internet. Divine command gives believers strong guidance but needs shared reasons at work. Consequentialism judges actions by results; utilitarianism seeks the greatest total good, act-style for single actions, rule-style for general rules. It is practical and fair in counting everyone equally, but struggles with prediction, measurement and justice for minorities. Next lesson we meet theories that look at duties, rights, contracts and character instead.
key_points: Ethical theories give a structured way to reason so others can follow and check your steps.
Subjective relativism makes disagreement meaningless and cannot condemn anyone; cultural relativism cannot explain moral progress.
Consequentialism judges actions by their results; utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill) seeks the greatest total good.
Applying utilitarianism: list stakeholders, list options, score benefits and harms, add up, pick the highest total.
Act utilitarianism judges each single action; rule utilitarianism judges the general rule if everyone followed it.
Weaknesses: consequences are hard to predict, happiness is hard to measure, and minorities can be treated unjustly.
Ethical egoism (act only for yourself) fails as a professional ethic because codes put the public first.
lessons.tip: When you answer a utilitarian exam question, draw a small table with stakeholders as rows and options as columns. Examiners love seeing the reasoning laid out.
lessons.task: Pick a real decision: should your class group chat allow anonymous posts? List at least 4 stakeholder groups, give each a score from -10 to +10 for 'allow' and 'don't allow', multiply by group size, and see which option wins. Then write one sentence on what the numbers missed.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with subjective relativism?
options: It makes moral disagreement meaningless and cannot criticise anyone
It only works for religious people
quiz.explain: If everyone is right for themselves, disagreements cannot be settled and even harmful acts cannot be criticised.

quiz.q: Who are the two philosophers most linked to utilitarianism?
quiz.explain: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill developed classic utilitarianism.

quiz.q: In the CCTV example, students score -3 each and there are 8,000 students. What is their total?
quiz.explain: -3 x 8,000 = -24,000, which dominated the total for Option A.

quiz.q: Rule utilitarianism asks...
options: Whether this single act makes things better right now
Which general rule would give the best results if everyone followed it
quiz.explain: Rule utilitarianism evaluates general rules, which avoids many terrible single-act conclusions.

quiz.q: Which is a known weakness of utilitarianism?
options: It can justify harming a minority if the total good goes up
It counts rich people's happiness more
It cannot be applied to any real case
quiz.explain: Because it adds up total good, it can sometimes approve unjust treatment of a small group.

lessons.title: Ethical Theories II: Duties, Rights, Contracts and Character
lessons.content:
Imagine your friend lends you 500 taka and says, 'Pay me back on Friday.' On Friday you meet a beggar and realise that giving him the 500 taka would make him much happier than your rich friend would be to get it back. A pure utilitarian calculation might say: give it to the beggar. But something inside you says: 'No, I promised.' That feeling, that some things are right or wrong no matter how the numbers turn out, is the starting point of the theories in this lesson. They look at duties, rights, agreements and the kind of person you are, not only at results.

Deontology: The word comes from the Greek 'deon', meaning duty. Deontological theories say some actions are right or wrong in themselves, because of what they are, not because of what they cause. Lying is wrong because it is a lie, not just because it may lead to bad results. Keeping a promise is a duty even when breaking it would be convenient. Where utilitarianism asks 'what will happen?', deontology asks 'what must I do, and what must I never do?'

Immanuel Kant: The most famous deontologist is the German philosopher Immanuel Kant (1724 to 1804). Kant believed morality comes from reason, not feelings or results. A good person acts from good will, meaning they do the right thing because it is right, not because it pays. If a shopkeeper gives correct change only because cheating might hurt business, he is acting prudently, not morally, in Kant's sense. Kant tried to find a single test for right action. He called it the categorical imperative: a command that applies to everyone, always, with no 'if you want X' attached.

First formulation, universal law: Act only according to a rule (Kant called it a maxim) that you could want to become a universal law for everyone. Test it in three steps. Step 1, state your rule clearly. Step 2, imagine everyone in the world followed it. Step 3, ask whether that world is even possible, or whether your rule would destroy itself. Example: 'I will make a false promise when I need money.' If everyone did that, nobody would believe promises any more, so false promises would stop working. The rule defeats itself, so it is wrong.

Worked test on a computing rule: Rule: 'I will use someone else's Wi-Fi password without asking whenever I find it.' Universalise: everyone uses any password they find. Result: people would lock everything down and stop sharing passwords at all, and the trust that makes shared Wi-Fi possible collapses. Another rule: 'I will copy code from classmates and submit it as my own.' Universalise: everyone does it. Then grades would mean nothing, and copying would stop giving you any advantage. Self-defeating again. Compare: 'I will credit every library I use.' Universalise: a world where everyone credits sources works perfectly well. That rule passes.

Second formulation, people as ends: Act so that you treat people always as ends in themselves, never merely as means. This means you may use people's help (a rickshaw puller takes you home, you pay him fairly, and he chooses the deal), but you must never use people like tools, ignoring their own goals and choices. Deceiving someone is using them merely as a means, because they never got to agree to the real deal. Hidden tracking, tricking users into subscriptions and dark patterns in apps all fail this test, because they use the user's attention or data without real consent.

Strengths of Kant: It protects individuals: you cannot sacrifice one innocent person just because numbers favour it, so the organ-harvesting surgeon from the last lesson is clearly wrong. It values honesty and consent, which are central to computing ethics. It treats everyone as equal rational beings, rich or poor. And it is consistent: the same rule for you as for everyone else, which stops people from making special exceptions for themselves.

Weaknesses of Kant: Duties can conflict. If a murderer asks where your friend is hiding, Kant's strict rule against lying seems to say you must not lie, which most people find absurd. Kant gives no clear way to rank conflicting duties. It can also ignore results too much: following a rule perfectly while a disaster happens feels wrong. And how you phrase the rule matters: 'lie to save a life' universalises better than 'lie whenever convenient', so clever phrasing can change the answer.

Rights: A close cousin of deontology is rights theory. A right is a justified claim that others must respect. Negative rights are rights to be left alone: the right not to be hurt, not to be spied on, to speak freely. They mainly require others to not interfere. Positive rights are rights to receive something: the right to education or basic healthcare. They require someone to provide. In computing, privacy is mostly discussed as a negative right (don't collect or expose my data), while internet access is increasingly discussed as something closer to a positive right. Rights act like fences: even if trespassing would raise total happiness, you may not cross them without a very strong reason.

Social contract theory: This family says morality is the set of rules that rational people would agree to, for their mutual benefit, if they had to live together. Thomas Hobbes (1588 to 1679) imagined life without any rules, a 'state of nature' where everyone fights everyone and life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. To escape, people agree to give up some freedom and obey shared rules, enforced by a government. Rules like 'don't steal' and 'keep promises' are part of this contract, because everybody benefits when everybody follows them.

Rawls and the veil of ignorance: In 1971 John Rawls published 'A Theory of Justice', a modern social contract theory. He asked: what rules would people choose if they did not know who they would be in society, rich or poor, man or woman, majority or minority, able-bodied or disabled? He called this choosing behind a veil of ignorance. Since you might end up as anyone, you would choose fair rules. Rawls argued people would pick two principles: equal basic liberties for everyone, and social and economic inequalities allowed only if they benefit the least advantaged (the difference principle) and come with fair equality of opportunity.

Using the veil in design: The veil is a powerful design tool. Imagine designing a mobile banking app without knowing whether you will be a young programmer in Gulshan, a garment worker who can barely read, an old man with shaky hands, or a blind student. You would insist on large buttons, voice support, Bangla text, simple PINs with good security, and low data use. In other words, the veil pushes you toward accessibility and inclusion, ideas we return to in lesson 25.

Virtue ethics: The oldest of these theories comes from Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE). Instead of asking 'which action is right?', virtue ethics asks 'what kind of person should I be?' A virtue is a good character trait built by practice, like honesty, courage, fairness, kindness and practical wisdom. Aristotle saw many virtues as a middle between two extremes: courage sits between cowardice and recklessness. You become honest by practising honesty, the way you become a good batsman by practising batting. For professionals, virtue ethics fits well: we want engineers who are honest, careful, humble about their limits and brave enough to speak up.

Strengths and weaknesses of virtue ethics: It explains moral growth and why habits matter. It values practical wisdom, the skill of seeing what a situation really needs. But it gives less precise guidance: 'be honest and wise' does not tell you exactly what to do when two good values clash. And people may disagree about which traits are virtues. In practice it combines well with the other theories.

Comparing all theories on one case: A startup in Chattogram finds that its health app accidentally exposed 2,000 users' test results for six hours. Nobody seems to have noticed. Should they tell the users? Utilitarian: telling users lets them protect themselves and keeps long-term trust; hiding risks a bigger scandal later; total good favours telling. Kantian: a rule 'hide breaches when nobody notices' cannot be universalised without destroying trust in all apps, and hiding treats users merely as means; telling is a duty. Rights: users have a right to know about risks to their private data. Social contract and Rawls: behind the veil you might be one of the 2,000, so you would choose a rule requiring notice. Virtue: an honest, courageous company tells. All theories agree here: tell the users. When theories agree, you can be confident. When they disagree, you have found a genuinely hard case that needs careful thought.

Real-life example 1, a ride-sharing surge: During heavy rain in Dhaka, a ride app's algorithm multiplies prices by 3. Utilitarian view: higher prices bring more drivers onto wet roads, so more people get home. Kantian and Rawlsian view: a nurse finishing a night shift may not afford 3 times the fare; behind the veil, would you accept unlimited surges? Many companies settle on a compromise: surge with a cap, shown clearly before booking. Seeing all lenses helps you find middle solutions, not just yes or no.

Real-life example 2, the exam proctoring app: A university wants to use an online exam app that watches students through their webcams and flags 'suspicious' eye movements. Kant: students are used as means if they are not told how the data is used. Rights: privacy inside one's own home. Utilitarian: cheating reduced, but anxious and disabled students may be wrongly flagged. Virtue: a fair institution explains the system, allows alternatives and lets humans review flags. The final design: clear notice, human review, data deleted after the exam.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students often write that Kant cares about results; he does not, he cares about the rule and the will. Another mistake is mixing up the two formulations: universal law is about the rule being universalisable; ends-not-means is about respecting people. Some forget that rights theory distinguishes negative and positive rights. Typical questions: 'State and apply Kant's categorical imperative to a case', 'Explain Rawls' veil of ignorance', 'Compare utilitarianism and Kantianism on a computing dilemma', 'What is virtue ethics?'

Recap: Deontology judges actions by duty; Kant's categorical imperative asks whether your rule can be universal law and whether you treat people as ends, never merely as means. Rights are fences others must respect, negative or positive. Social contract theory sees morality as rules rational people would agree to; Rawls's veil of ignorance pushes toward fairness for the least advantaged. Virtue ethics focuses on character built by practice. Use several lenses together: agreement gives confidence, disagreement shows where to think harder. Next lesson turns these lenses into a practical step-by-step decision method.
key_points: Deontology judges actions by duty: some acts are right or wrong in themselves, regardless of results.
Kant's first formulation: act only on a rule you could will to be a universal law; self-defeating rules are wrong.
Kant's second formulation: treat people as ends, never merely as means; deception and hidden tracking fail this test.
Negative rights require others not to interfere; positive rights require someone to provide something.
Social contract theory (Hobbes, Rawls): morality is the rules rational people would agree to; the veil of ignorance pushes toward fairness.
Virtue ethics (Aristotle) asks what kind of person to be; virtues are traits built by practice.
Use several theories together: if all agree you can be confident; disagreement marks a genuinely hard case.
lessons.tip: Memorise one short computing example for each theory (for example: false promise for Kant, accessibility for Rawls). Examiners reward a correct theory applied to a concrete case far more than a long definition.
lessons.task: Take the rule 'I will share my Netflix or Spotify password with friends'. Apply Kant's universal law test in three written steps, then apply the veil of ignorance from the point of view of a small Bangladeshi music artist. Do the two answers agree?

lessons.title: Making Ethical Decisions Step by Step
lessons.content:
When a doctor sees a patient with a fever, she does not guess. She follows a routine: ask questions, check temperature, look for other symptoms, consider possible causes, choose a treatment, and follow up. The routine stops her from missing something important when she is tired or rushed. Ethical problems at work need the same kind of routine. They usually arrive at bad moments: on a Thursday night before a launch, in a tense meeting, in a message from your boss. If you have a step-by-step method ready, you can think clearly instead of panicking or going along with the crowd.

What an ethical dilemma is: Not every hard decision is an ethical dilemma. Choosing between Flutter and React Native is a technical choice. An ethical dilemma appears when values clash, for example honesty against loyalty to your team, users' privacy against company profit, or speed against safety. Often there is no option that keeps everyone fully happy. The goal of a method is not to make the dilemma disappear, but to make sure you have seen it clearly and can defend your choice.

Why a method helps: Our gut feelings are useful but biased. We favour people we like, we avoid conflict, and we believe convenient stories. Psychologists have shown that people under time pressure and authority pressure often do things they later regret. A written method slows you down just enough to catch these biases. It also gives you something to show others: 'Here are the facts, here are the options, here is why I chose this one.'

Step 1, recognise the ethical issue: Notice that there is one. Warning signs: you feel uncomfortable; someone says 'don't tell anyone'; a decision affects people who are not in the room; you would not want the decision to appear in the newspaper; the words 'just this once' are used. Many disasters happen not because people chose evil, but because nobody noticed the moment was ethical at all.

Step 2, get the facts: What exactly is happening? What do we know and what are we guessing? Who decided what, and when? What are the laws, company policies and contracts involved? Facts can dissolve a dilemma. Maybe the 'secret' data sharing was actually in the privacy policy that users agreed to. Or facts can make it worse: maybe the 'small' bug affects payments. Write the facts down separately from opinions.

Step 3, identify the stakeholders: List everyone affected and what each one has at stake. Users, their families, colleagues, the company, shareholders, regulators, the wider public, future users. Ask: who is most vulnerable? Who has no voice in this decision? In Bangladesh, for example, many users of mobile financial services are not tech-savvy, so they are more vulnerable to confusing design or hidden fees.

Step 4, list the options: Do not stop at two options. Most people think 'do it' or 'refuse and quit', but there are almost always more. You can ask questions, propose a safer alternative, delay, escalate to a senior person, add a warning, limit the feature, or document your concern. Aim for at least four options. Creative middle options are often the best answer.

Step 5, test each option: Run each option through several tests. The harm test: does this option do less harm than the others? The publicity test, also called the front-page test: would I be comfortable if this decision and my reasons appeared on the front page of a newspaper or went viral on Facebook? The reversibility test: would I still think it is fair if I were the person on the receiving end? The universality test, from Kant: what if everyone in my position did this? The code test: what does the ACM or IEEE code say (lesson 06)? The legal test: is it legal? The colleague test: what would a respected senior engineer say?

Step 6, decide and justify: Pick the option that does best across the tests, not necessarily the one that wins only one test. Write a short justification in plain language. If you cannot explain your choice without embarrassment, that is a signal to look again.

Step 7, act, and then reflect: Act on the decision in a professional way: calm, factual, respectful, in writing where possible. Afterwards, reflect. What happened? What would you do differently? What can the team change so the dilemma does not come back? Good organisations turn individual dilemmas into better processes, for example by adding a privacy review to every new feature.

A compact way to remember: Some teachers use the letters of a short phrase. One simple version: Notice, Facts, People, Options, Tests, Decide, Reflect. Seven steps, one line each. You can write them on a sticky note on your monitor.

Worked case, the hidden bug before launch: You are a developer at a Dhaka fintech startup. Launch is tomorrow at 10 a.m., with a big press event. Tonight you find a bug: if two transfers are sent within 1 second from the same account, sometimes the balance is reduced only once. Your test shows it happens in about 1 of every 2,000 double-transfers. Your manager says: 'Ship it. We'll patch it next week. Don't mention it to the CEO, it will just cause stress.'

Applying the steps, part 1: Notice: 'Don't mention it' is a red flag. Facts: the bug lets money be created out of nothing, which is a financial integrity problem; about 1 in 2,000 double-transfers fail. If 40,000 double-transfers happen in the first week, expected failures are 40,000 / 2,000 = 20. Each could be abused once people discover it, and fraudsters share tricks quickly. Stakeholders: users, the company, its bank partner, the regulator, the CEO who will answer for it, you. Options: (a) ship silently; (b) ship and tell the CEO; (c) delay launch; (d) ship with a quick block on transfers less than 2 seconds apart, a small change you can test tonight; (e) refuse and resign.

Applying the steps, part 2: Tests. Option (a) fails the publicity test badly: 'Startup hid known money bug at launch.' Option (e) is dramatic and probably unnecessary. Option (c) is safe but costly. Option (d) plus (b) looks strongest: it reduces harm right away, keeps the launch, and tells the decision-maker the truth. Decision: implement the 2-second guard, test it, and send a short factual email to your manager and, if needed, the CEO, describing the bug, the temporary guard and the plan for a full fix. Reflection: add a concurrency test for transfers to the release checklist.

Rationalisations, the traps: People who do wrong things rarely think 'I am being evil'. They tell themselves a story. Learn the common stories so you can catch them in your own head. 'Everybody does it.' 'It's not my job.' 'Nobody will find out.' 'It's legal, so it's fine.' 'The boss told me to.' 'It's just a small thing.' 'We'll fix it later.' 'They agreed to the terms and conditions.' 'If I don't do it, someone else will.' Each of these can be true and still be no reason at all. When you hear one, slow down and go back to step 2.

Pressure and obedience: In the 1960s the psychologist Stanley Milgram ran famous experiments in which many ordinary volunteers obeyed an authority figure's instructions to give what they believed were painful electric shocks to another person (the shocks were fake). The lesson most people draw is that authority pressure is powerful, and good people can do harmful things when someone in charge takes the responsibility. In workplaces this is why codes of ethics insist that you keep your own responsibility, even under orders.

When you are unsure: Ask for advice early. Talk to a trusted senior colleague, a mentor, a teacher, or the company's ethics or compliance contact if there is one. Describe the situation without names if needed. Sleep on it if time allows: many bad decisions are made in the first emotional hour. Keep notes with dates; if things go wrong later, a clear record protects honest people.

How to raise a concern well: Being right is not enough; you also need to be heard. Speak to the person closest to the decision first, privately, before going over their head. Stick to facts and impact ('this bug can let a balance go negative') rather than blame ('you are careless'). Bring at least one solution, not only a problem. Put the key points in a short email afterwards so there is a record, for example: 'As discussed, I found X, the risk is Y, I suggest Z.' If nothing happens and the risk is serious, move one level up, and say openly that you are doing so. This calm, step-by-step escalation solves most workplace dilemmas long before anyone needs to think about whistleblowing, which we study in lesson 07.

Real-life example 1, the group project: Your university group of four must submit a software project. One member never worked but wants equal marks. Notice: fairness issue. Facts: commit history shows zero commits from him. Stakeholders: you, the others, him, the teacher. Options: cover for him, report him, talk to him first and give a final chance, ask the teacher for a fair contribution policy. Tests point to talking first, then informing the teacher with evidence if nothing changes. This is far better than secretly removing his name, or doing nothing and resenting him.

Real-life example 2, the freelance website: A client on a freelancing platform asks you, a Bangladeshi developer, to build a website that copies a famous brand's design and logo exactly, to sell cheaper 'similar' products. Facts: copying a logo raises trademark problems (lesson 11). Stakeholders: the client, the brand, buyers who may be misled, you and your rating. Options: refuse, build an original design instead, explain the risk. Tests: the front-page test and the legal test both fail for copying. The professional answer is to offer an original design and explain why, which often keeps the client.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students often jump straight to a decision without listing options, or list only two options. Others forget to separate facts from assumptions. In exam case studies, examiners look for: a clear statement of the ethical issue, a list of stakeholders, several options, analysis with at least two ethical theories or tests, a justified decision, and preventive steps. Answers that only say 'it is unethical' without reasons score low.

Recap: An ethical dilemma is a clash of values. A method protects you from bias and pressure: notice the issue, get facts, identify stakeholders, list several options, test them (harm, front-page, reversibility, universality, code, law, colleague), decide and justify, act professionally and reflect. Watch for rationalisations like 'everyone does it' and 'the boss told me'. Next lesson asks what it means to be a professional at all, and what society expects from people who call themselves engineers.
key_points: An ethical dilemma is a clash of values, such as honesty versus loyalty or profit versus privacy.
A written method protects against bias, time pressure and authority pressure.
Seven steps: notice, get facts, identify stakeholders, list options, test options, decide and justify, act and reflect.
Aim for at least four options; creative middle options are often best.
Useful tests: harm, front-page (publicity), reversibility, universality, professional code, law, respected colleague.
Rationalisations like 'everybody does it', 'the boss told me' and 'we'll fix it later' are warning signs, not reasons.
Milgram's experiments showed how strongly authority pressure can push ordinary people to do harm.
lessons.tip: Write the seven steps on a sticky note and practise them on small everyday dilemmas. When a big dilemma arrives, the habit will already be there.
lessons.task: Choose a dilemma you have seen (for example, a friend asking for your assignment file). Write it up using all seven steps on one page, with at least four options and at least three tests applied to each.

options: A situation where important values clash
quiz.explain: A dilemma involves a clash of values, like honesty against loyalty, not just a technical choice.

quiz.q: The 'front-page test' asks...
options: Would I be comfortable if this decision and my reasons were published?
quiz.explain: The publicity or front-page test checks whether you would be comfortable having the decision made public.

quiz.q: A bug fails in 1 of every 2,000 double-transfers. With 40,000 double-transfers, how many failures are expected?
quiz.explain: 40,000 / 2,000 = 20 expected failures.

quiz.q: Which of these is a rationalisation, not a real reason?
options: The fix reduces harm to users
quiz.explain: 'Everybody does it' is a classic rationalisation; it says nothing about whether the act is right.

quiz.q: Why should you list more than two options?
options: Creative middle options are often better than simply doing it or quitting
More options make the decision faster
quiz.explain: Thinking beyond 'do it or quit' often reveals safer middle paths.

lessons.title: What It Means to Be a Professional
lessons.content:
When you get on a bus in Dhaka, you trust the driver knows how to drive. When you cross a flyover, you trust the engineers calculated the loads correctly. When you take medicine, you trust the pharmacist gave the right one. You cannot check any of this yourself. Modern life runs on trust in people who know things we do not. That trust is the heart of what we call a profession. Software engineers are now part of this circle of trust: your money, your health records and even your car's brakes depend on code you will never read. This lesson asks: what makes someone a professional, and what does society expect in return for its trust?

Job, occupation, profession: A job is any work you are paid for. An occupation is a general type of work, like driving or tailoring. A profession is a special kind of occupation with extra features: it needs a long education, it serves important public needs, its members have a lot of independence, and it has its own ethical standards. Classic examples are medicine, law and civil engineering. People argue about whether software engineering is fully a profession yet, and the arguments themselves teach you a lot.

Feature 1, specialised knowledge: Professionals master a body of knowledge that takes years to learn and that ordinary people cannot easily check. A patient cannot judge a surgeon's technique. A shop owner using a billing app cannot judge whether its database is safe. This knowledge gap creates power, and power creates responsibility. Because clients cannot protect themselves, the professional must protect them.

Feature 2, education and continuing learning: Professions require formal education, often a degree, plus practical experience. Doctors do internships; lawyers do pupillage or bar exams. In computing, a BSc in CSE is the usual entry, but the field changes so fast that what you learn in first year may be outdated by graduation. So a true professional keeps learning for a whole career: new languages, new security threats, new laws. This is called continuing professional development, or CPD.

Feature 3, autonomy: Professionals are trusted to make judgments on their own. A doctor decides the treatment; the hospital manager does not. In software, senior engineers decide architecture, security design and whether code is ready to ship. With autonomy comes accountability: if you made the call, you answer for it.

Feature 4, a code of ethics and self-regulation: Every true profession has a written code of ethics and some way to discipline members who break it. Medical councils can remove a doctor's registration. In computing, organisations like the ACM and IEEE have codes (lesson 06), but they usually cannot stop someone from working as a programmer, because in most countries, including Bangladesh, there is no compulsory licence to write software. This is the biggest reason people say software is a 'young' or 'partial' profession.

Feature 5, public service and trust: Professions exist because society needs something important done well: health, justice, safe buildings. In return, society gives professionals status, decent pay and freedom. If professionals abuse that trust, society takes the freedom back by adding strict laws. This is a social contract (lesson 03) between a profession and the public.

Why professions build codes and rules: History shows a pattern. A new skill appears, people start selling it, some of them do it badly or dishonestly, the public gets hurt, and then either the practitioners organise themselves with standards and codes, or the government steps in with strict laws. Civil engineering went through this after bridge and building collapses; medicine went through it as quack doctors harmed patients. Computing is somewhere in the middle of this story. Every major software failure or data scandal adds pressure for stronger rules. Engineers who behave well today are, in a sense, deciding whether the profession stays mostly self-regulated or gets regulated from outside.

Certification versus licensing: These two words are often confused. Certification is voluntary: an organisation tests you and gives you a certificate saying you have certain skills. Examples in computing include vendor certificates for cloud platforms and networking, and security certificates. You can work without them, but they help you get hired. Licensing is compulsory and given by the government or a legally empowered body: without a licence you are not allowed to practise. Doctors and lawyers need licences. Most software work does not. Some places have experimented with licences for software engineers working on safety-critical systems, but this is not common worldwide.

Should software engineers be licensed? Arguments for: software now controls planes, pacemakers, power grids and money, so incompetent work can kill people or ruin them; licensing would set a minimum standard; the public could identify qualified people. Arguments against: software is extremely varied, so one exam cannot cover web design and avionics; the field changes too fast for a fixed exam; licensing could block self-taught talent and people from poorer backgrounds; much software is built by large teams where blame is shared. A balanced view many people hold: licensing may make sense for safety-critical domains, while most other software relies on certification, company processes and codes of ethics.

Professional bodies worldwide: The ACM (Association for Computing Machinery), founded in 1947, is the largest scientific and educational computing society; it runs conferences, journals, the Turing Award and the ACM Code of Ethics. The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) and its Computer Society cover electrical, electronic and computer engineering, publish standards (Wi-Fi is the IEEE 802.11 family) and have their own code. In the UK, the BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT, offers chartered status for IT professionals.

Professional bodies in Bangladesh: Several organisations matter for a Bangladeshi computing graduate. The Bangladesh Computer Society (also shortened to BCS, not to be confused with the UK one or the civil service exam) is a professional society for ICT people. BASIS, the Bangladesh Association of Software and Information Services, is the trade body of the software and IT services industry. The Institution of Engineers, Bangladesh (IEB) is the national body for engineers in many disciplines. Student chapters of ACM and IEEE exist at many Bangladeshi universities, and joining one is an easy way to meet the professional world early.

Competence: The first duty of a professional is to be competent: to do only work you are qualified for, or to get qualified first, or to bring in someone who is. Suppose a client asks a web developer to build a payment gateway, and she has never studied security. Honest options: say 'I do not have that skill', learn it properly before starting, or partner with a security expert. The unprofessional option is to fake it. Competence also means knowing your limits on a particular day: tired, rushed work on a critical system is a competence problem too.

Duty of care and due diligence: In law and ethics, a professional owes a duty of care to people who rely on their work: they must act with the care a reasonable, skilled professional would use. Due diligence means doing the reasonable checks before acting: testing, code review, reading the documentation, checking the licence of a library, backing up before a migration. If you skip normal checks and someone is harmed, you may be found negligent, which we study in lesson 08.

Responsibilities to different groups: A professional has duties pulling in different directions. To the public: safety, honesty and well-being come first. To clients and employers: loyalty, confidentiality, doing the agreed job well. To the profession: keeping its reputation, mentoring juniors, sharing knowledge. To colleagues: credit, fairness, respect. To yourself: keep learning, keep healthy limits. When these conflict, most codes agree the public interest comes first.

Professional and employee at the same time: Most software engineers are employees, not independent professionals like a doctor with her own clinic. This creates a built-in tension. As an employee, you follow your manager's instructions and protect the company's business interests. As a professional, you must also protect the public and refuse to do clearly harmful or dishonest work. Most days there is no conflict: building a good product serves both. The tension shows up at the edges, for example when a deadline pushes you to skip security testing. Knowing that both roles exist helps you notice the edge before you cross it, and reminds you that 'I was only an employee' does not cancel your professional duty.

Real-life example 1, the government tender: A small Dhaka software firm wins a tender to digitise land records for a district. The team has never built a system with such sensitive data and such strict audit needs. A professional firm would: admit gaps and hire or consult experts in security and data management; plan backups and audit logs from the start; test with real officials; train staff; and document everything. An unprofessional firm would deliver a quick demo and leave. Land records decide who owns land, so a careless system can cause real disputes and even violence. Competence is not optional here.

Real-life example 2, the hospital app: A young developer builds a medicine reminder app for a private hospital in Sylhet. A doctor asks her to add a feature that suggests doses automatically. She knows code, not medicine. Professional behaviour: refuse to invent dosing rules herself; ask the hospital to provide rules approved by qualified doctors; add clear warnings; and log every suggestion so a doctor can review it. She stays inside her competence and makes the boundary visible to everyone.

The professional mindset in daily work: Professionalism shows up in small habits more than in grand speeches. Write clear commit messages. Do code reviews honestly, not just clicking 'approve'. Estimate time truthfully instead of promising what you know is impossible. Admit your own bugs quickly. Protect passwords and test data. Treat junior colleagues and interns with patience. Answer client questions honestly, even when the answer is 'I don't know yet'. Over a career, these habits build a reputation that is worth more than any certificate.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students mix up certification (voluntary) and licensing (compulsory, legal). Others write that software engineering is 'not a profession at all'; a better answer explains which features it has (specialised knowledge, codes, public impact) and which are weak (compulsory licensing, enforcement). Exams often ask: 'List the characteristics of a profession', 'Should software engineers be licensed? Argue both sides', 'Explain competence and duty of care with an example', 'Name professional bodies relevant to computing'.

Recap: A profession needs specialised knowledge, long education with lifelong learning, autonomy, a code of ethics with self-regulation, and a public-service purpose based on trust. Software engineering has most of these but usually no compulsory licence. Certification is voluntary, licensing is legal permission. Key duties are competence, duty of care and due diligence, with the public interest first. Next we read the actual codes of ethics written by the ACM and IEEE.
key_points: A profession needs specialised knowledge, formal education with lifelong learning, autonomy, a code of ethics with self-regulation, and public trust.
The knowledge gap between professionals and clients creates power, and that power creates responsibility.
Certification is voluntary proof of skill; licensing is compulsory legal permission to practise.
Most software work, including in Bangladesh, needs no compulsory licence, which is why software is called a young or partial profession.
Major bodies: ACM, IEEE, UK's BCS; in Bangladesh: Bangladesh Computer Society, BASIS, IEB, and university ACM/IEEE chapters.
Competence means doing only work you are qualified for, learning first, or bringing in an expert.
Duty of care and due diligence mean doing the reasonable checks a skilled professional would do.
lessons.tip: Join your university's ACM or IEEE student chapter, or attend a local tech event. Seeing professionals in person makes 'professionalism' concrete and builds your network early.

options: Accept and learn while coding in production
Admit the gap, learn properly first, or bring in a security expert
quiz.explain: Competence means doing only work you are qualified for or getting qualified or help first.

lessons.title: Codes of Ethics: ACM, IEEE and the Software Engineering Code
lessons.content:
Every cricket team has a written rulebook, but good teams also have an unwritten spirit: you walk off when you know you edged the ball, you do not sledge a debutant into tears, you help an injured opponent up. Professional codes of ethics try to write down the spirit of a profession, so that newcomers can learn it quickly and members can point to it when under pressure. If your manager asks you to hide a known safety bug, it is much easier to say 'Section 1.2 of the ACM Code says avoid harm' than 'I just feel bad about it.' This lesson reads the main computing codes, shows how to use them on a case, and explains what codes cannot do.

What a code of ethics is: A code of ethics is a written statement, made by a professional body, of the values and responsibilities its members should follow. It is different from a law: breaking it usually does not send you to prison, though a body can expel you. It is different from company rules: it applies wherever you work. Think of it as the profession's shared conscience, written down.

Why codes exist: Codes do several jobs at once. They inspire members to aim high. They educate newcomers about expectations they might not guess. They give support: an employee can cite the code to refuse an unethical order. They help the public know what to expect. They can be used to judge members accused of misconduct. And writing a code forces a profession to discuss and agree on its values, which is useful in itself.

The ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct: The ACM, the largest computing society, updated its code in 2018. It has four sections. Section 1 gives general ethical principles. Section 2 lists professional responsibilities. Section 3 covers leadership principles for people who manage others. Section 4 covers compliance with the code itself. Each item is a short headline followed by a paragraph of explanation, so you can quote the headline and then explain it in your own words.

ACM Section 1, general principles: There are seven. 1.1 Contribute to society and to human well-being, acknowledging that all people are stakeholders in computing. 1.2 Avoid harm. 1.3 Be honest and trustworthy. 1.4 Be fair and take action not to discriminate. 1.5 Respect the work required to produce new ideas, inventions, creative works and computing artifacts. 1.6 Respect privacy. 1.7 Honor confidentiality. Notice how these map onto earlier lessons: 1.1 and 1.2 echo utilitarian concern for well-being, 1.3 echoes Kant's ban on deception, 1.4 echoes Rawls's fairness, and 1.5 leads to intellectual property (lessons 10 to 12).

What 'avoid harm' really means: The code explains that harm includes physical, mental and financial injury, unjust damage to property and reputation, and harm to the environment. It also says harm can be unintended, so professionals should consider possible consequences in advance and act to reduce unintended harm. Crucially, it adds a duty to report: if you see signs that a system might cause harm, you should take reasonable steps to report it. Ignorance is not a full excuse if you could reasonably have known.

ACM Section 2, professional responsibilities: There are nine. 2.1 Strive for high quality in both the processes and products of professional work. 2.2 Maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct and ethical practice. 2.3 Know and respect existing rules about professional work, including laws, and challenge unethical rules through proper channels. 2.4 Accept and provide appropriate professional review. 2.5 Give comprehensive and thorough evaluations of computer systems and their impacts, including possible risks. 2.6 Perform work only in areas of competence. 2.7 Foster public awareness and understanding of computing. 2.8 Access computing and communication resources only when authorised or when compelled by the public good. 2.9 Design and implement systems that are robustly and usably secure.

ACM Sections 3 and 4: Section 3 is for leaders: 3.1 ensure the public good is the central concern during all professional computing work; plus duties to set good policies, improve working life for staff, create learning opportunities, take care when changing or retiring systems people depend on, and take special care with systems that become part of society's infrastructure. Section 4 says members should uphold and promote the code, and that violating it is inconsistent with ACM membership.

The Software Engineering Code: In 1999, a joint task force of the ACM and the IEEE Computer Society approved the Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice. It has eight principles, each with a list of detailed clauses. The eight keywords are easy to memorise: Public, Client and Employer, Product, Judgment, Management, Profession, Colleagues, Self.

The eight principles in plain words: 1, Public: act consistently with the public interest. 2, Client and Employer: act in the best interests of your client and employer, consistent with the public interest. 3, Product: make sure your products and changes meet the highest professional standards possible. 4, Judgment: keep integrity and independence in your professional judgment. 5, Management: managers should promote an ethical approach to managing software development and maintenance. 6, Profession: advance the integrity and reputation of the profession. 7, Colleagues: be fair to and supportive of colleagues. 8, Self: keep learning throughout life and promote an ethical approach to the practice. Notice the order: Public comes first, and Client and Employer is limited by 'consistent with the public interest'.

The IEEE Code of Ethics: The IEEE has a shorter code, revised several times. Its central promise is to hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public, and to disclose promptly factors that might endanger the public or the environment. It also asks members to protect privacy, avoid real or perceived conflicts of interest, be honest and realistic in claims and estimates, reject bribery, maintain technical competence and take on tasks only when qualified, seek and offer honest criticism, admit and correct errors, credit others properly, treat all people fairly without discrimination or harassment, and support colleagues who follow the code, without retaliating against people who report violations.

What the codes agree on: Put the three codes side by side and the same core ideas appear: public safety and welfare first; honesty in claims, estimates and results; competence and continued learning; privacy and confidentiality; fairness and no discrimination; respect for others' work and proper credit; and the courage to report risks. If you remember these seven ideas, you will be right about almost any code question.

Using a code on a case, worked: A Rajshahi startup builds a crop-loan app for farmers. Your manager wants the default interest display to show the monthly rate (2 percent) in large text and hide the yearly equivalent. Compound yearly cost: 1.02 to the power 12 is about 1.268, so about 26.8 percent per year, compared with a naive 24 percent. Which code clauses apply? ACM 1.3 honesty; ACM 1.2 avoid harm, since farmers may borrow more than they can repay; ACM 1.4 fairness, since less-educated users are the most misled; SE Code principle 1, Public, and principle 3, Product. Decision: show the yearly cost clearly beside the monthly rate, with a worked example in Bangla, and explain to the manager using the code. The code turns 'I feel uneasy' into specific, quotable reasons.

Quoting a code at work, a sample: Codes are most useful when written into a calm message. For example: 'Hi Rafiq bhai, I am worried that showing only the monthly rate may mislead farmers about the real yearly cost (about 26.8 percent). The ACM Code asks us to be honest (1.3) and to avoid harm (1.2), and our users include many first-time borrowers. Could we show the yearly cost next to the monthly rate? I can make the change today.' Notice the parts: the concern, the fact, the clause, the affected users, and a ready solution. A message like this is hard to dismiss and easy to agree with, and it leaves a polite written record.

Limits of codes: Codes are not magic. They are general, so they do not decide every case. Clauses can conflict: confidentiality to a client against warning the public. They usually lack enforcement: most programmers are not ACM or IEEE members, and losing membership does not stop someone from working. Some people treat codes as public relations, signing them without reading them. And codes can lag behind technology, which is why the ACM rewrote its code in 2018 after 26 years. A code is a starting point for reasoning, not a replacement for it.

Company codes of conduct: Most large companies also have their own codes of conduct, covering gifts, conflicts of interest, harassment, data handling and use of company property. Banks and mobile financial services in Bangladesh, for example, typically make staff sign rules about customer confidentiality. These codes are often enforceable through employment contracts, so breaking them can cost you your job. Read your company code in your first week; most people never do.

Real-life example 1, the face filter: A Dhaka app team adds a 'beauty' filter that automatically lightens skin tones. A junior engineer notices complaints that it suggests lighter skin is more beautiful. ACM 1.4 (be fair, do not discriminate) and 1.1 (human well-being) apply, and 2.5 asks for thorough evaluation of impacts. The professional step is to raise it with evidence, propose a filter that preserves skin tone, and test it with diverse users. Many global apps faced exactly this criticism.

Real-life example 2, the stolen dataset: A classmate offers you a leaked database of 100,000 phone numbers and names to test your SMS marketing project. ACM 2.8 (access resources only when authorised), 1.6 (respect privacy) and 2.3 (respect laws) all say no. Using synthetic, generated test data solves the technical need without harm. Codes help you see that 'just for testing' does not change whose data it is.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students list code items without applying them; examiners want you to quote the relevant clause and then explain how it applies. Others confuse the ACM Code (general computing, 2018) with the Software Engineering Code (1999, eight principles). Remember the eight keywords in order. Typical questions: 'State five principles of the ACM Code', 'List the eight principles of the SE Code', 'Apply a code of ethics to the following case', 'What are the limitations of professional codes?'

Recap: A code of ethics writes down a profession's values. The ACM Code (2018) has general principles (1.1 to 1.7), professional responsibilities (2.1 to 2.9), leadership principles and compliance. The ACM and IEEE-CS Software Engineering Code has eight principles from Public to Self, with Public first. The IEEE Code holds public safety, health and welfare paramount. Codes inspire, educate and support, but they are general, can conflict and are weakly enforced. Next lesson takes the codes into real workplace dilemmas: conflicts of interest, gifts, loyalty and whistleblowing.
key_points: A code of ethics is a profession's written statement of values; it is not law, but bodies can expel members.
ACM Code (2018) sections: general principles, professional responsibilities, leadership principles, compliance.
ACM general principles: contribute to well-being, avoid harm, be honest, be fair, respect creative work, respect privacy, honour confidentiality.
The ACM/IEEE-CS Software Engineering Code (1999) has eight principles: Public, Client and Employer, Product, Judgment, Management, Profession, Colleagues, Self.
The IEEE Code holds paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public.
All codes agree on public first, honesty, competence, privacy, fairness, credit and reporting risks.
Codes are general, can conflict, are weakly enforced and lag technology; they guide reasoning but do not replace it.

They are laws that send violators to prison
