lessons.title: Workplace Dilemmas: Conflicts of Interest, Gifts, Loyalty and Whistleblowing
lessons.content:
Imagine you are the referee in a local football final, and your younger brother plays for one of the teams. Even if you are perfectly fair, everyone on the other side will suspect every whistle you blow. That is a conflict of interest in its simplest form: your personal connection pulls against the job you are supposed to do fairly. Workplaces are full of smaller versions of this, along with gifts that feel like bribes, secrets you must keep, bosses you want to be loyal to, and sometimes wrongdoing you cannot ignore. This lesson is about those everyday and not-so-everyday dilemmas.

Conflict of interest, what it is: A conflict of interest happens when a personal interest (money, family, friendship, a side business) could influence, or could look like it influences, a professional judgment you make for someone else. Example: you choose software vendors for your bank, and one vendor is your cousin's company. You might choose fairly, but your judgment is no longer clearly independent. The IEEE Code asks members to avoid real or perceived conflicts of interest and to disclose them when they exist.

Actual, potential and perceived conflicts: An actual conflict is happening now: you are scoring tenders and your cousin's bid is on the table. A potential conflict could happen soon: your cousin plans to bid next month. A perceived conflict is one that others may reasonably believe exists, even if you are sure it does not affect you. All three matter, because trust depends on how things look as well as on how they are.

Handling a conflict, step by step: Step 1, notice it early. Step 2, disclose it in writing to your manager or the relevant committee. Step 3, step back (recuse yourself) from the decision, so someone without the conflict decides. Step 4, if the conflict is permanent, remove it, for example by selling shares in a supplier. Disclosure plus recusal solves most cases. The serious mistake is hiding the conflict and hoping nobody finds out.

Side work and moonlighting: Many Bangladeshi developers do freelance work on top of a full-time job. This is often fine, but check three things: does your employment contract allow it; are you using company time, laptops or code; and are you working for a competitor or a client of your employer? Using your employer's code in a freelance project can also break confidentiality and copyright, because code written as part of your job usually belongs to the employer.

Gifts and hospitality: Small gifts are part of normal business and culture: a box of sweets at Eid, a calendar at New Year, lunch during a meeting. The question is whether a gift could influence your decisions or look like it does. Useful tests: Is it small and occasional? Would you be comfortable telling your manager? Is it given openly or secretly? Is it connected to a decision you are about to make? Many companies set a value limit and require you to register gifts above it.

Bribery: A bribe is anything of value given to influence an official or business decision improperly: cash, an expensive phone, a foreign trip, a job for a relative. Bribery is unethical everywhere and illegal in most countries; in Bangladesh, corruption is investigated by the Anti-Corruption Commission. In IT, bribery often hides inside procurement: a vendor pays someone to write tender requirements that only their product can meet. A professional refuses, reports it and documents it. The IEEE Code says plainly: reject bribery in all its forms.

A worked gift check: A vendor offers you, the team lead choosing a database platform, (a) a branded pen, (b) a free ticket to a public technical conference that everyone in your role gets, (c) a smartwatch worth 25,000 taka during the evaluation, (d) a paid holiday for your family. Apply the tests: (a) small, open, not linked to a decision, acceptable; (b) probably fine if open and approved, since it is educational and not personal; (c) high value, during a decision, refuse; (d) clearly a bribe, refuse and report. The timing and value matter as much as the item.

Confidentiality: Professionals learn secrets: source code, business plans, customer data, security weaknesses. ACM 1.7 says honor confidentiality. You must not share these without permission, even after you leave the job. Many contracts include a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), covered more in lesson 11. Confidentiality has a limit: it does not require you to hide crimes or serious dangers to the public. The ACM Code explicitly says confidentiality can be overridden when the law requires it or when evidence shows serious harm.

Loyalty: Being loyal to your employer is a real virtue: working hard, protecting its reputation, not badmouthing it in public, not stealing its clients. But loyalty is not blind obedience. A loyal engineer warns the company about risks, because a company that ships a dangerous product will be harmed too. Philosophers often distinguish loyalty to the company's legitimate goals from loyalty to a particular boss's bad decision. When they clash, the professional codes put the public first.

Changing jobs cleanly: Software engineers in Bangladesh often move between companies, and that is healthy. The ethical line is between what is in your head and what belongs to your old employer. Your general skills, experience with a language, and knowledge of good design patterns are yours to take. Source code, customer lists, internal documents, passwords and confidential plans are not. Before leaving, return laptops, delete company files from personal devices, and hand over your work properly so the team is not left stuck. At the new job, do not offer your old company's secrets as a way to impress, and say no if someone asks. A new employer who wants stolen secrets today will not respect your loyalty tomorrow.

Whistleblowing, what it is: Whistleblowing means an insider reporting serious wrongdoing in their organisation to people who can act on it. Internal whistleblowing goes to higher management, an ethics committee or an internal hotline. External whistleblowing goes outside: a regulator, the police, the media. External whistleblowing is a serious step, because it can damage the organisation and the whistleblower's own career.

When is whistleblowing justified? A common set of conditions, from ethicist Richard De George's writing on whistleblowing, goes like this. It is permitted when: the organisation's product or policy will do serious and considerable harm to the public; you have reported it to your immediate supervisor; and you have used the internal channels up to the top without result. It becomes a stronger obligation when, in addition, you have documented evidence that would convince a reasonable outsider, and you have good reason to believe going public will actually prevent the harm. These conditions are a guide, not a law, but they explain why whistleblowing should usually come after internal efforts.

A classic case, Challenger: In January 1986, the US space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing seven crew members. Engineer Roger Boisjoly and colleagues at the contractor had warned the night before that rubber O-ring seals might fail in the unusually cold weather. Their warnings were overruled by managers under schedule pressure. After the disaster, Boisjoly testified to the investigating commission about the warnings. The case is taught everywhere because it shows engineers who raised concerns correctly, managers who overrode them, and the cost of ignoring technical judgment.

Computing cases: In 2013 Edward Snowden, a contractor for the US National Security Agency, leaked documents showing large-scale surveillance programs; people still argue fiercely about whether he was a hero or a lawbreaker, which makes it a useful debate case. In 2021 Frances Haugen, a former Facebook product manager, shared internal research with regulators and journalists about harms of the platform. These cases show the high personal cost of external whistleblowing: legal risk, lost careers, exile in Snowden's case.

Protection for whistleblowers: Many countries have laws to protect people who report wrongdoing in the public interest. Bangladesh passed a public-interest information disclosure (whistleblower protection) act in 2011. Protection usually depends on reporting through the right channels and in good faith. Before going external, learn which law applies and, if possible, get legal advice. Good companies also protect internal reporters with anonymous hotlines and a clear rule against retaliation.

Harassment and fair treatment: Ethical workplaces also mean treating colleagues fairly: no discrimination by gender, religion, ethnicity, disability or background; no bullying; no sexual harassment. In Bangladesh, a 2009 High Court guideline requires workplaces and educational institutions to have measures and complaint committees against sexual harassment. Both the ACM and IEEE codes forbid harassment. If you see it, support the target and report it through proper channels.

Remote work and freelancing ethics: Remote and freelance work bring new temptations: billing hours you did not work, running two full-time jobs secretly, using AI or subcontractors without telling a client who paid for your personal work, or quietly reusing one client's code for another. Simple rule: bill honestly, disclose who does the work, keep each client's code and data separate, and respect contracts. Your platform rating is built on trust over years, and one dishonest invoice discovered by a client can undo it in a single review.

Real-life example 1, the procurement committee: A Dhaka hospital forms a committee to buy a new patient-record system. A committee member's brother-in-law owns one of the bidding software firms. Correct path: the member discloses the relationship in the first meeting, the minutes record it, and he leaves the room for that bid's evaluation. Nobody's reputation is harmed, and the purchase stays clean.

Real-life example 2, the hidden data sale: A developer at a lifestyle app discovers the company is selling users' precise location history to a data broker, contrary to its own privacy policy. She raises it with her lead, then with the CTO, with written evidence. Nothing changes. Before considering external reporting, she checks the law, keeps copies only of what she is entitled to keep, and seeks advice. Following the steps in order protects both the public and herself.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students think a conflict of interest means you did something wrong; it only means a risk exists, and disclosing it is the right move. Others confuse whistleblowing with gossip or with leaking for personal revenge. Exams ask: 'Define conflict of interest and explain how to handle it', 'Distinguish internal and external whistleblowing', 'State conditions under which whistleblowing is justified', 'Discuss the Challenger case'.

Recap: Conflicts of interest (actual, potential, perceived) are handled by disclosure and recusal. Small open gifts can be fine; valuable gifts tied to decisions and all bribes must be refused. Confidentiality is a duty with limits for crime and serious public harm. Loyalty means serving legitimate goals, not blind obedience. Whistleblowing should usually follow exhausted internal channels, with evidence, and with awareness of legal protection. Next lesson looks at what happens when software fails: reliability, liability and accountability.
key_points: A conflict of interest is when a personal interest could influence, or seem to influence, your professional judgment.
Conflicts can be actual, potential or perceived; handle them by early written disclosure and stepping back from the decision.
Judge gifts by value, timing, openness and link to a decision; refuse bribes in every form.
Confidentiality is a strong duty but does not require hiding crimes or serious danger to the public.
Loyalty means serving the company's legitimate goals, not blindly obeying a bad decision.
Whistleblowing is usually justified only for serious harm, after internal channels are exhausted, with solid evidence.
Bangladesh has a 2011 whistleblower protection law; protection depends on good faith and proper channels.
lessons.tip: Start a habit now: whenever you make a decision that involves a friend or relative, write one line disclosing it to whoever is affected. It costs nothing and builds a reputation for fairness.

lessons.title: When Software Fails: Reliability, Liability and Accountability
lessons.content:
When a building collapses, investigators ask hard questions. Was the design wrong? Was cheap cement used? Did an inspector sign without looking? Who is responsible, and who must pay? Software can fail just as badly, but its failures are often invisible until the moment they hurt someone, and the blame is easy to scatter: 'the computer did it'. This lesson studies famous software failures, what caused them, and the ideas of reliability, liability and accountability that society uses to decide who answers for harm.

Why software fails: Software fails for a small set of reasons that repeat again and again. Wrong or missing requirements: the system does what was asked, but what was asked was wrong. Design errors: the structure cannot handle real conditions. Coding errors: off-by-one mistakes, race conditions, overflow. Poor testing: important cases never tried. Reuse without re-checking: code that was safe in an old setting fails in a new one. Bad user interfaces: operators misunderstand what the system is doing. Overconfidence: removing human or hardware checks because 'the software is reliable'. And organisational pressure: deadlines that push people to skip all of the above. You learned many technical defences in Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4) and Software Testing (deep-cse-5-8); here we focus on the human and ethical side.

Reliability versus safety: Reliability is the probability that a system works correctly for a given time under given conditions. Safety is freedom from unacceptable risk of harm. They are related but not the same. A system can be reliable and unsafe: a radiation machine that very reliably delivers a wrong dose. A system can be safe but unreliable: a cash machine that often refuses to work but never gives wrong money. Ethically, safety-critical systems (medical, aviation, transport, power, finance) deserve the most care.

Case 1, Therac-25: Therac-25 was a radiation therapy machine made by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Between 1985 and 1987, at least six known accidents gave patients massive radiation overdoses, and several patients died or were seriously injured. Investigators, especially Nancy Leveson and Clark Turner in their 1993 report, found several causes. Earlier models had hardware interlocks that physically prevented dangerous settings; Therac-25 removed them and trusted software alone. A race condition meant that if an experienced operator edited the treatment settings quickly, the machine could enter a dangerous state. Error messages were cryptic, such as 'MALFUNCTION 54', and operators learned to just press 'proceed'. The company at first insisted overdoses were impossible. Lessons: never remove safety layers just because software exists, design clear error messages, test for fast human input, and take user reports seriously.

Case 2, Ariane 5 Flight 501: On 4 June 1996, Europe's new Ariane 5 rocket destroyed itself about 37 seconds after launch. The inertial reference software, reused from the smaller Ariane 4, converted a 64-bit floating-point value related to horizontal velocity into a 16-bit signed integer. Ariane 5 flew faster, the number became larger than 32,767, the largest a 16-bit signed integer can hold, and an unhandled overflow error shut down the system. The backup unit ran the same software and failed the same way. Lessons: reused code must be re-verified for its new environment, and identical backups do not protect against identical bugs.

Case 3, the Patriot missile clock: In February 1991, during the Gulf War, a Patriot missile battery in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia failed to intercept an incoming Scud missile, which hit a US army barracks and killed 28 soldiers. The system counted time in tenths of a second, but 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary, so each tick lost about 0.000000095 seconds. After about 100 hours of continuous running, that is 100 x 3600 x 10 = 3,600,000 ticks, and the error grew to about 3,600,000 x 0.000000095 = 0.34 seconds. A Scud travels roughly 1,676 metres per second, so the tracking gate was off by more than 500 metres. A software fix was already on its way. Lessons: tiny numeric errors grow with time, and operational limits ('reboot regularly') must be clearly communicated.

Case 4, Boeing 737 MAX: In October 2018 (Lion Air Flight 610) and March 2019 (Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302), two Boeing 737 MAX planes crashed, killing 346 people. A flight control feature called MCAS could push the nose down repeatedly based on a single angle-of-attack sensor; when that sensor gave a false reading, pilots fought the system. Investigations criticised the design's reliance on one sensor, the limited information given to pilots, and pressures in certification. The fleet was grounded worldwide for about 20 months. Lessons: single points of failure in safety systems are dangerous, users must understand automation that can override them, and commercial pressure must not weaken safety review.

Case 5, the Post Office Horizon scandal: In the UK, an accounting system called Horizon was used in post office branches from around 1999. It sometimes showed cash shortfalls that did not really exist. Hundreds of sub-postmasters were prosecuted for theft or false accounting, some went to prison, and many lost their savings, while the organisation insisted the system was reliable. Years later, courts found the system had bugs and the convictions began to be overturned. Lessons: never assume 'the computer is always right', give people a fair way to challenge system outputs, and remember that a bug can destroy lives without any physical accident.

Accountability, responsibility, liability: These three words sound similar but mean different things. Responsibility is about roles and duties: who was supposed to do what. Accountability means being answerable: you must explain and justify what happened, and accept consequences, even if you were not at fault in the legal sense. Liability is a legal idea: who must pay damages or face punishment under the law. An engineer can be morally responsible without being legally liable, and a company can be liable even if no single person is to blame.

The many hands problem: Philosopher Helen Nissenbaum, in a 1996 paper, described barriers to accountability in computing. The first is many hands: software is built by large teams, so when it fails, everyone can say 'it was someone else's part'. The second is bugs: people treat bugs as natural and unavoidable, like weather, rather than as mistakes. The third is the computer as scapegoat: 'the system did it'. The fourth is ownership without liability: companies claim full rights over software but disclaim responsibility for harm. Knowing these barriers helps you resist them: keep clear records of who decided what, treat bugs as preventable, and do not hide behind the machine.

Negligence: In law, negligence means failing to take the care a reasonable person or professional would take, causing harm. It usually needs four elements: a duty of care existed; the duty was breached (the care fell below the standard); the breach caused the harm; and real damage resulted. Example: a developer of a hospital billing system skips basic input validation that every reasonable developer would include, and patients are overcharged. Duty, breach, causation and damage are all present.

Warranties and disclaimers: A warranty is a promise about a product's quality, for example 'this app will calculate VAT correctly'. Many software licences include disclaimers like 'provided AS IS, without warranty of any kind', trying to limit liability. Courts in different countries treat such disclaimers differently; consumer protection laws often limit how much a seller can disclaim, especially for consumers. Ethically, a disclaimer does not erase your duty to build carefully. It only shifts legal risk.

Product liability and contracts: When a defective product injures someone, many legal systems make the maker liable, sometimes even without proving negligence (this is called strict liability). Whether software counts as a 'product' for these rules differs between countries and is still debated, especially for software inside physical devices like cars and medical equipment. For custom software, contracts usually define responsibilities, testing, acceptance and limits of liability. Reading and negotiating these clauses is part of professional practice, covered more in Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11).

Safety standards: Because failures in some fields are so costly, industries have written safety standards for software. IEC 61508 is a general standard for safety-related electronic systems. DO-178C guides software in aircraft. ISO 26262 covers road vehicles, and IEC 62304 covers medical device software. These standards do not guarantee perfection, but they force teams to classify how dangerous each failure would be, match the amount of testing and review to that danger, keep traceable records from requirements to tests, and have independent people check the work. Following the relevant standard is part of what a court or investigator would see as 'reasonable care' in that field.

What good engineers do: Use defence in depth: hardware interlocks, software checks and human review together. Avoid single points of failure in safety functions. Re-verify reused code. Design clear errors and safe defaults. Test edge cases, timing and long runs. Log decisions and keep records of who approved what. Report incidents honestly and learn from them with blameless post-mortems, which focus on fixing causes rather than punishing individuals. And speak up early when deadlines threaten safety, using the methods from lesson 04.

Real-life example 1, a Bangladeshi utility bill: Imagine a prepaid electricity meter system in a Bangladeshi city suddenly deducts double charges for thousands of homes after an update. Families run out of credit at night. Who is accountable? The vendor who wrote the update, the utility that deployed it without testing, the manager who approved it under deadline. A mature response: stop the rollout, refund automatically, publish a clear explanation, and add an approval step and automated billing tests. Nobody hides behind 'system error'.

Real-life example 2, the exam result bug: A board's result processing software mixes up two students' marks because of a sorting bug when names are identical. One student is shown failed. The ethical response is not just to fix the code but to create a fast, free process for students to challenge results, because affected people need a path to correction. Horizon showed what happens when that path is missing.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students confuse reliability and safety, or responsibility and liability. Others describe Therac-25 only as 'a software bug', forgetting the removed hardware interlocks, poor error messages and organisational denial. Exams often ask: 'Discuss the causes and lessons of Therac-25', 'Explain the Ariane 5 failure', 'Define negligence and its elements', 'What is the many hands problem?', 'Should software makers be liable for defects?'

Recap: Software fails through wrong requirements, design and coding errors, weak testing, unchecked reuse, poor interfaces, overconfidence and pressure. Therac-25, Ariane 5, the Patriot clock, the 737 MAX and Horizon show these causes in real lives. Reliability is working correctly; safety is freedom from unacceptable harm. Responsibility is about roles, accountability is answering for outcomes, liability is legal. Nissenbaum's barriers explain why blame scatters. Negligence needs duty, breach, causation and damage. Good engineers build layered defences and own their mistakes. Next lesson turns to honesty in study and research: plagiarism and academic integrity.
