Therac-25 removed hardware interlocks, had a race condition and cryptic errors, and caused massive radiation overdoses (1985 to 1987).
Ariane 5 (1996) failed when reused code overflowed a 16-bit integer; the identical backup failed the same way.
Reliability means working correctly; safety means freedom from unacceptable risk of harm.
Responsibility is about roles, accountability is answering for outcomes, liability is legal duty to pay or be punished.
Nissenbaum's barriers: many hands, bugs seen as natural, computer as scapegoat, ownership without liability.
Negligence requires duty, breach, causation and damage; disclaimers shift legal risk but not ethical duty.
lessons.tip: For each famous case, learn three things: what happened, the technical cause, and the human or organisational cause. Exam answers that include all three score highest.
lessons.task: Calculate the Patriot clock drift yourself: error per tick 0.000000095 s, 10 ticks per second. How large is the error after 8 hours, 20 hours and 100 hours? Write one sentence on what this teaches about long-running systems.

quiz.q: What important safety feature did Therac-25 remove compared with earlier models?
quiz.explain: Earlier models had hardware interlocks; Therac-25 relied on software alone, so software errors became deadly.

quiz.q: Why did Ariane 5 Flight 501 fail?
options: A 64-bit value overflowed when converted to a 16-bit signed integer in reused code
quiz.explain: Reused Ariane 4 code could not handle Ariane 5's larger values, and the backup had the same bug.

quiz.q: Which four elements are usually needed to prove negligence?
quiz.explain: Negligence requires a duty of care, a breach of it, harm caused by that breach, and actual damage.

quiz.q: 'Everyone on a big team can say it was someone else's part' describes...
quiz.explain: Nissenbaum's 'many hands' barrier explains how blame scatters in large software teams.

quiz.q: A system that very reliably delivers a wrong, dangerous dose is...
quiz.explain: Reliability and safety are different; consistent behaviour can still be dangerous.

lessons.title: Academic Integrity and Plagiarism
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket tournament where some batsmen secretly use bats with a hidden metal core. Their scores shoot up, they win awards, and honest players are left behind. Soon nobody trusts any big score. The whole tournament loses its meaning. Universities work the same way. A degree is a promise to employers and society: this person really learned these things. Every copied assignment and faked lab result weakens that promise for everyone, including the honest students. Academic integrity means keeping that promise true. This lesson explains what counts as cheating, why it matters even for 'small' assignments, how plagiarism in code is detected, and how to use sources and AI tools honestly.

What academic integrity is: Academic integrity is acting honestly, fairly and responsibly in learning and research. The International Center for Academic Integrity describes it with values like honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. In practice it means: the work you submit as yours is really yours, you give credit for every idea and piece of text or code you used, you report data as it really was, and you follow the rules your teacher set for each task.

Why it matters beyond grades: First, learning: if you copy the sorting assignment, you never learn sorting, and that gap shows up in interviews and on the job. Second, fairness: honest classmates compete with you for grades, scholarships and jobs. Third, trust in your degree: if a university becomes known for cheating, employers stop trusting its graduates. Fourth, habits: people who cut corners in student life often cut corners at work, where the stakes are users' money and safety. Integrity is professional training that starts on day one.

Plagiarism, the definition: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words, ideas, code, images or data as your own, without proper credit. Intention does not change the definition much: careless copying without citation is still plagiarism, though penalties may differ. It applies to essays, reports, slides, code, diagrams and even ideas you heard in a seminar.

Types of plagiarism: Direct or copy-paste plagiarism: copying text or code word for word without credit. Mosaic or patchwork plagiarism: mixing copied phrases with your own words and changing a few words here and there, so it looks original. Paraphrasing without credit: rewriting someone's idea in your own words but not citing the source, which is still taking their idea. Self-plagiarism: submitting your own earlier work again as new without permission, for example reusing last semester's project for a new course. Contract cheating: paying or asking someone else to do your work, including online 'assignment help' services. Collusion: working together when the task was meant to be individual.

Collaboration versus collusion: Discussing ideas with friends is good learning. The line is drawn by your teacher's rules. A common, safe rule: you may discuss the problem and general approaches, but you write your own code and words, and you do not look at or share actual solution files. If you are helped a lot by someone, say so in your submission ('I discussed the recursion idea with Nabila'). When rules are unclear, ask the teacher before, not after.

When a friend asks for your file: This is the most common integrity dilemma in Bangladeshi universities. Giving your solution file to a friend who 'just wants to see the idea' usually makes you part of the collusion, and both submissions get flagged. A kinder and safer option is to explain the idea on a whiteboard or paper, then let your friend write their own code. You help them learn, and you protect both of you.

Code plagiarism: Code is easy to copy and seems easy to disguise. Students rename variables, change comments, reorder functions, or swap a for loop for a while loop. These tricks do not change the underlying structure, and that structure is what detection tools look at. Copying code from a public website or a senior's old repository without credit is plagiarism too, even if the code is open source, because the assignment asks for your work.

How code similarity detection works: A well-known system is MOSS (Measure Of Software Similarity), created at Stanford by Alex Aiken in the 1990s and widely used in universities. The idea, simplified: Step 1, turn the program into a stream of tokens and normalise it, so every variable name becomes the same symbol and comments and spacing are removed. Step 2, cut the token stream into overlapping groups of k tokens, called k-grams. Step 3, hash each k-gram and keep a selected subset of hashes as the program's fingerprint (MOSS uses a method called winnowing to choose them). Step 4, compare fingerprints between all pairs of submissions and report pairs that share many fingerprints, highlighting the matching parts for a human to review.

A tiny worked example: Student A writes 'sum = sum + arr[i]'. Student B writes 'total = total + arr[i]'. After normalisation both become 'V = V + V [ V ]', identical token streams, so renaming bought nothing. Now suppose two different programs each produce 6 distinct 3-token groups, and 2 of them are shared. A simple similarity measure, the Jaccard index, is shared divided by total distinct: 2 / (6 + 6 minus 2) = 2 / 10 = 0.2, or 20 percent, which is normal for independent solutions of the same small task. Two copied programs would score close to 100 percent. Tools only flag; a teacher still judges, because short, standard code (like a for loop over an array) can match naturally.

Text plagiarism detection: Services like Turnitin compare submitted text against huge databases of web pages, books, journals and earlier student submissions, and produce a similarity report. A high percentage is not automatically plagiarism: quoted and cited text also matches. A low percentage does not prove innocence either: clever paraphrasing or translation can hide copying. Like code tools, they help a human decide.

Citing and referencing: Citation means pointing to your source inside the text; referencing means listing full details at the end. Computing usually uses the IEEE style, with numbers in square brackets like [1], or APA style, with author and year like (Rahman, 2021). Cite when you use a direct quotation (also put it in quotation marks), a paraphrased idea, data, a figure, or code. In code, put a comment above borrowed parts: '// Adapted from: URL, accessed on date, licence MIT'. You do not need to cite common knowledge, such as 'Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh' or 'binary search runs in O(log n)'.

Good paraphrasing: To paraphrase well, read the source, close it, write the idea from memory in your own structure and words, then check you did not copy phrases, and still cite the source. Changing every fifth word while keeping the sentence structure is not paraphrasing; it is mosaic plagiarism.

AI tools and integrity: Generative AI tools can write essays and code. Universities' policies differ: some ban AI for certain tasks, some allow it with disclosure, some encourage it for brainstorming. The integrity principles stay the same: follow the specific rules of each course; never submit AI output as if you wrote it when the task asks for your own work; disclose how you used it ('I used an AI assistant to explain the error message; all code is mine'); and check the output, because AI can invent facts and fake references. Fake references are a serious integrity breach even if a tool produced them.

Research misconduct: In research, the three classic forms are fabrication, falsification and plagiarism, often abbreviated FFP. Fabrication is making up data or results that were never obtained. Falsification is manipulating experiments, equipment or data, or leaving out results, so the record is not accurate, for example deleting test runs where your algorithm performed badly. Plagiarism is as above. A famous case: physicist Jan Hendrik Schön at Bell Labs published many celebrated papers around 2000 to 2002 before investigators found fabricated data; many papers were withdrawn. Research ethics is covered more in Research Methodology (deep-cse-7-7) and writing skills in Technical Writing (deep-cse-6-8).

Consequences: Penalties range from zero marks on the assignment, to failing the course, to suspension or expulsion, and for research misconduct, retracted papers and lost careers. Degrees have been revoked years later when plagiarism in a thesis was discovered. Beyond formal penalties, trust once lost is hard to rebuild: teachers write recommendation letters, and they remember.

Why students cheat, and how to avoid the trap: Studies of academic dishonesty keep finding the same triggers: too little time, fear of failing, unclear rules, the belief that 'everyone does it', and a feeling that the task is pointless. Notice that most of these are planning problems, not character problems. Practical defences: start assignments on the day they are given, even for 20 minutes, so the deadline never becomes a panic; ask the teacher early when you are stuck, because a late submission with a small penalty is far better than a copied one with a zero and a record; and remind yourself why the task exists. A sorting assignment feels pointless until a job interview asks you to sort without a library.

Real-life example 1, the lab report: A student in a Dhaka university finds a senior's lab report on Data Communication with almost the same experiment. He changes the name, some numbers and the conclusion, and submits it. The similarity tool flags 78 percent matching with last year's submission database. Investigation shows the measured values were not from his own experiment, so it is both plagiarism and fabrication. The honest path: run the experiment, record real values even if messy, and cite the senior's report if he used its structure, with permission.

Real-life example 2, the programming contest: In a university programming contest, a team copies a solution from a public online judge during the contest, against the rules. Similarity checks after the contest catch it, and the team is disqualified. In contests and in jobs, the rule is the same: know what help is allowed, and stay within it.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students think citing makes any amount of copying fine; if most of your work is quoted, it is still not your work. Others think changing variable names avoids detection; normalisation removes names. Some think self-plagiarism is impossible; reusing your own work without permission is a breach. Exams ask: 'Define plagiarism and list its types', 'Distinguish collaboration from collusion', 'How do code plagiarism detectors work?', 'What are fabrication and falsification?', 'How should AI tools be used honestly?'

Recap: Academic integrity means honest, fair work with credit given. Plagiarism includes copying, patchwork, uncredited paraphrase, self-plagiarism, contract cheating and collusion. Code detectors normalise tokens, hash k-grams into fingerprints and compare them, so renaming does not hide copying, and humans make the final call. Cite with IEEE or APA style and comment borrowed code. Use AI only as allowed and disclose it. In research, avoid fabrication, falsification and plagiarism. Next we move to the law of ownership of ideas: intellectual property, starting with copyright.
key_points: Academic integrity means submitting your own work, crediting all sources, reporting real data and following each task's rules.
Plagiarism is presenting others' words, ideas, code or data as your own; it includes copy-paste, mosaic, uncredited paraphrase, self-plagiarism, contract cheating and collusion.
Collaboration is discussing ideas within the rules; collusion is sharing work when it should be individual.
Code detectors like MOSS normalise tokens, hash k-grams into fingerprints and compare them, so renaming variables does not hide copying.
Similarity scores only flag; a human must judge, because cited quotes and standard code match naturally.
Use AI tools only as each course allows, disclose use, and check output for invented facts and fake references.
Research misconduct is fabrication, falsification and plagiarism (FFP).
lessons.tip: Keep a 'sources.txt' file in every project folder from day one and paste each link or book you use, with the date. Writing references at the end becomes a two-minute job instead of a panic.
lessons.task: Take two short code snippets that do the same thing written by you and a friend. Replace every variable name with V, remove comments, split into 3-token groups and compute the Jaccard similarity by hand.

quiz.q: Rewriting someone's idea in your own words without citing them is...
options: Fine, because the words are yours
Plagiarism, because the idea is still theirs
quiz.explain: Paraphrasing without credit still presents another person's idea as yours.

quiz.q: Why does renaming variables not fool tools like MOSS?
options: MOSS normalises identifiers into the same token before comparing
quiz.explain: Normalisation turns all names into one symbol, so the structure is compared, not the names.

quiz.q: Two programs each have 6 distinct 3-grams and share 2. What is their Jaccard similarity?
quiz.explain: Union = 6 + 6 - 2 = 10, so Jaccard = 2/10 = 0.2.

quiz.q: Deleting the test runs where your algorithm performed badly is an example of...
quiz.explain: Falsification is manipulating or omitting data so the record is inaccurate.

quiz.q: What is the honest way to use an AI assistant on a course that allows it?
options: Submit its output as your own without mention
Follow the course rules, disclose how you used it and check its output
Use it only for references, which are always correct
Hide it because teachers cannot detect it
quiz.explain: Integrity needs rule-following, disclosure and verification, since AI can invent facts and references.

lessons.title: Intellectual Property I: Copyright
lessons.content:
Imagine you spend three months writing a Bangla song, recording it in your room and uploading it. A week later, a big company uses it in a TV advertisement without asking you or paying you. You would feel robbed, even though you still have your song. Nothing was physically taken, yet something valuable was. Intellectual property law exists for exactly this kind of situation. It treats creations of the mind, like songs, books, inventions, logos and software, as a kind of property that the creator controls for a while. This lesson covers the most important form for programmers: copyright.

What intellectual property is: Intellectual property (IP) means legal rights over creations of the mind. The main types are copyright (creative works including software), patents (inventions), trademarks (brand names and logos), trade secrets (valuable confidential information) and industrial designs (the look of a product). This lesson is about copyright; lesson 11 covers the others and lesson 12 covers software licences.

Why IP exists, the core argument: Ideas and digital works are unusual: if I eat your mango, you cannot eat it, but if I copy your song, you still have it. Economists say such goods are non-rival. They are also hard to exclude: once published, anyone can copy them. Without any protection, a writer who spends a year on a book could be undercut by a printer who copies it in a day and sells it cheaper. Fewer people would invest in creating. So society gives creators a temporary exclusive right, as an incentive to create and share. When the right ends, the work becomes free for everyone. This bargain, temporary control in exchange for eventual public benefit, is the heart of IP.

The other side of the argument: Some argue that strong IP can also slow down creativity and access. Students in poor countries may not afford textbooks or software, and new artists build on older works. That is why copyright has limits: it lasts only for a time, it protects expression but not ideas, and it allows certain fair uses. Thinking about both sides is part of ethics, not just law.

What copyright protects: Copyright protects original works of authorship that are fixed in some form: books, articles, songs, films, photos, drawings, architecture plans, and computer programs. Original means the work came from the author's own effort and choices, not copied; it does not need to be brilliant. Fixed means it exists in some form: written, recorded, saved in a file. An unrecorded speech in your head is not protected.

Idea versus expression: The most important rule: copyright protects the expression of an idea, not the idea itself. Anyone may write a story about a poor boy who becomes a cricket star; nobody may copy someone else's actual text of such a story. In software, the idea of a ride-sharing app, a sorting algorithm or a menu layout is not protected by copyright, but the specific source code someone wrote is. This is why two companies can build similar apps legally, as long as they write their own code.

Automatic protection: Under the Berne Convention, an international treaty from 1886 that most countries have joined, copyright arises automatically when a work is created and fixed. You do not need to register it or put a copyright symbol on it. Registration, where available, is optional but useful as evidence in a dispute. Bangladesh has a Copyright Office where works, including software, can be registered. The notice '(c) 2025 Rahim Uddin' is still a helpful warning, but it is not what creates the right.

The rights copyright gives: The owner gets exclusive economic rights, meaning only they can do or permit these acts: reproduce the work (make copies); distribute copies; make adaptations or derivative works (translations, remixes, modified versions of software); perform or display it publicly; and communicate it to the public, including by putting it online. Many countries also recognise moral rights: the right to be named as the author and the right to object to distortions that harm the author's reputation. Moral rights often stay with the author even after selling the economic rights.

How long it lasts, worked: The Berne Convention sets a minimum term of the author's life plus 50 years for most works. Many countries, including the European Union members and the United States, use life plus 70 years. In Bangladesh, the general term for literary works has been the author's life plus 60 years; laws do get revised, so check the current version. Worked example: an author dies in 2000. Under life plus 60, protection runs until the end of 2060, and the work enters the public domain on 1 January 2061. Under life plus 70, that date becomes 1 January 2071. Works by companies, or anonymous works, often have terms counted from publication instead.

The public domain: Works whose copyright has expired, or that were never protected, are in the public domain. Anyone may copy, adapt and sell them. Rabindranath Tagore died in 1941, so his works have long been out of copyright in most countries, which is why many free editions exist. But be careful: a new translation, a new recording or a new edition with added notes can have its own fresh copyright.

Who owns it: Normally the author owns the copyright. But works made by employees as part of their job usually belong to the employer; this is often called work made for hire. So code you write at your job belongs to your company unless your contract says otherwise. For freelancers, ownership depends on the contract: if it does not clearly transfer copyright, the freelancer may still own it and only grant a licence. This is why good contracts state ownership explicitly.

Software and copyright: International agreements, especially the TRIPS Agreement of the World Trade Organization (1994), say computer programs, whether in source or object code, are protected as literary works. So copying someone's source code, or copying their compiled program and distributing it, can infringe copyright. Translating code into another language line by line can also be infringement, because it is an adaptation. Writing your own code that does the same thing, from your own understanding, is not.

Interfaces and the Google v. Oracle case: A famous question is whether APIs, the names and structure that programs use to talk to each other, are protected. In Google v. Oracle, Google had copied the declaring code (about 11,500 lines) of the Java API for Android. In 2021 the US Supreme Court decided Google's use was fair use, without deciding the bigger question of whether APIs are copyrightable at all. The case shows how expensive and uncertain these questions can be.

Fair use and fair dealing: Copyright allows some uses without permission. In the United States, fair use is judged by four factors: the purpose and character of the use (for example educational, critical, transformative or commercial), the nature of the work, the amount used, and the effect on the market for the original. In the UK, India, Bangladesh and many Commonwealth-style systems, the law lists specific permitted purposes, often called fair dealing, such as private study, research, criticism, review and news reporting. Quoting a paragraph from a book in your review, with credit, is usually fine. Uploading the whole book as a PDF is not.

Infringement and remedies: Infringement means doing one of the owner's exclusive acts without permission and without an exception. Remedies can include court orders to stop, damages, seizing copies, and in serious commercial cases criminal penalties. Online platforms commonly use notice-and-takedown systems: the owner reports infringing content and the platform removes it. YouTube's Content ID system automatically matches uploads against reference files from rights holders.

Digital locks and anti-circumvention: Because digital copying is so easy, owners often add technical protection, called digital rights management (DRM): encrypted e-books, streaming that cannot be downloaded, software activation keys. The 1996 WIPO Copyright Treaty asked member countries to protect these locks legally, and the United States did so in the Digital Millennium Copyright Act of 1998, which makes breaking such locks, or selling tools to break them, unlawful in many cases. Critics point out that DRM can also block legitimate uses, like a blind reader's screen reader or a researcher's security test, so some laws include exceptions. Cracking a game's licence check is therefore not only copying; it may be a separate offence.

Copyright and AI training: A very new question is whether training AI models on millions of copyrighted books, images and code is allowed. AI developers argue it is like a student learning from reading, or that it is a fair use. Many authors, artists and news organisations argue it copies their work without permission or payment. Courts in several countries are still deciding cases, and some new laws require AI developers to be more transparent about training data. The final answers are not settled yet, so treat any confident claim with caution, and when you build AI systems, prefer data you have clear rights to use.

Real-life example 1, the startup logo font: A Dhaka startup's designer downloads a beautiful paid font from a 'free fonts' site and uses it in the app and marketing. Fonts as software files are protected by copyright in many countries, and their licences often forbid commercial use without payment. The safe path: use fonts with clear licences, such as open-licensed fonts from reputable sources, or buy the licence. Checking takes five minutes; a dispute can take months.

Real-life example 2, the tutorial channel: A student starts a programming tutorial channel in Bangla. He uses short clips of a famous English course to illustrate points, adds his own explanations, credits the source, and keeps clips brief. This is closer to fair use or fair dealing for teaching and criticism. Another channel re-uploads full lectures with Bangla subtitles. That copies the whole work and can replace the original, so it is likely infringement, even with credit. Credit is good manners, but it is not permission.

Common mistakes and exam points: 'If I give credit, I can use anything.' No, credit is not permission. 'It's online, so it's free.' No, online works are protected by default. 'Copyright protects my app idea.' No, only your expression. 'I must register to be protected.' No, protection is automatic under Berne. Exams ask: 'What does copyright protect and for how long?', 'Explain the idea-expression distinction with a software example', 'What is fair use or fair dealing?', 'Who owns software written by an employee?'

Recap: IP gives creators temporary control over creations of the mind as an incentive, balanced by limits. Copyright protects original, fixed expression, not ideas, and arises automatically under the Berne Convention. It gives rights to reproduce, distribute, adapt, perform and communicate, plus moral rights. Terms are at least life plus 50 years, commonly life plus 70, and in Bangladesh traditionally life plus 60. Employers usually own employees' work. Software is protected as a literary work. Fair use and fair dealing allow limited uses such as study, criticism and news. Next lesson covers patents, trademarks, trade secrets and designs.
key_points: Intellectual property gives creators temporary exclusive rights as an incentive to create, after which works enter the public domain.
Copyright protects original, fixed expression, not ideas; the idea of an app is free, the code someone wrote is not.
Under the Berne Convention (1886), copyright is automatic; registration is optional evidence.
Rights: reproduce, distribute, adapt, perform or display, communicate to the public; plus moral rights of attribution and integrity.
Term: at least life + 50 years (Berne), often life + 70; Bangladesh has traditionally used life + 60, check the current law.
Work done by employees as part of their job usually belongs to the employer.
Fair use (US four factors) and fair dealing (listed purposes like study, research, criticism, news) allow limited use without permission.
lessons.tip: Whenever you use any image, font, music or code, ask two questions: 'Who owns this?' and 'What licence lets me use it?' If you cannot answer both, find something else.
lessons.task: Pick 5 items you might use in a project (a photo from Google Images, a YouTube music track, a GitHub library, a font, a book quote). For each, find out who owns it and what you would need to use it legally. Write one line per item.

quiz.q: Which is protected by copyright?
options: The idea of a food delivery app
A sorting algorithm as a concept
The specific source code someone wrote for an app
The general layout idea of a menu
quiz.explain: Copyright protects expression, like actual code, not ideas or methods.

quiz.q: Under the Berne Convention, when does copyright begin?
options: Automatically when an original work is created and fixed
Only after registration with the government
Only after the work is sold
quiz.explain: Berne requires automatic protection without formalities.

quiz.q: An author dies in 2000. Under life + 60, when does the work enter the public domain?
quiz.explain: Protection runs to the end of 2060, so it becomes public domain on 1 January 2061.

quiz.q: Code you write as part of your job usually belongs to...
quiz.explain: Work made by employees in the course of employment usually belongs to the employer unless the contract says otherwise.

quiz.q: Which statement about credit and copyright is correct?
options: Giving credit always makes copying legal
Credit is good practice but is not the same as permission
Only registered works can be infringed
quiz.explain: Attribution is ethical and often required, but you still need permission or an exception to copy.

lessons.title: Intellectual Property II: Patents, Trademarks, Trade Secrets and Designs
lessons.content:
Think about a bottle of a famous soft drink. The recipe inside is kept in a locked vault: a trade secret. The curvy shape of the bottle can be protected as a design. The name and logo on the label are trademarks. A clever new cap that keeps the fizz longer might be patented. And the advertisement jingle is protected by copyright. One small bottle, five kinds of intellectual property. Last lesson covered copyright. This lesson covers the other four, and shows where software fits into each.

Why different types exist: Each type of IP protects a different kind of value, and each makes a different bargain with society. Copyright protects expression and arises automatically. A patent protects a useful invention, but only if you apply and publish the details. A trademark protects a brand's identity for as long as it is used. A trade secret protects information only while it stays secret. Choosing the right protection is a business and ethical decision, and many products use several types at once.

Patents, what they are: A patent is an exclusive right granted by a government for an invention: a new product or process that offers a new technical solution. During the patent term, the owner can stop others from making, using, selling or importing the invention without permission. In exchange, the inventor must disclose the invention in a public document detailed enough for a skilled person to reproduce it. So the bargain is: a temporary monopoly in return for teaching the world how it works. When the patent ends, everyone may use it.

The three tests for a patent: Most patent systems, following the TRIPS Agreement, require three things. Novelty: the invention must be new, not already disclosed anywhere in the world before the filing date, including by the inventor's own earlier publication in many countries. Inventive step, also called non-obviousness: it must not be an obvious step for a skilled person in that field. Industrial application, also called utility: it must be capable of being made or used in some kind of industry. Mere discoveries of nature, abstract ideas, mathematical formulas and scientific theories are generally not patentable on their own.

Patent term, worked: Under TRIPS, the minimum patent term is 20 years from the filing date. Worked example: a Bangladeshi engineer files a patent for a low-cost water filter on 1 March 2010. If granted and the renewal fees are paid, it lasts until 1 March 2030. After that, anyone may make the filter. Notice it counts from filing, not from grant, so years spent waiting for examination use up the term.

How patents work in practice: Step 1, the inventor searches existing patents and publications (prior art) to check novelty. Step 2, a patent application is written with a description, drawings and claims; the claims are the precise legal boundaries of what is protected. Step 3, the patent office examines it, often asking for changes. Step 4, if granted, the owner pays renewal fees to keep it alive. Patents are territorial: a Bangladeshi patent protects only in Bangladesh. The Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) lets inventors start one international application and later choose countries. In Bangladesh, patents, designs and trademarks are handled by the Department of Patents, Designs and Trademarks (DPDT).

Software patents, the debate: Can software be patented? It depends on the country and the claim. In the United States, the Supreme Court's 2014 Alice decision said that taking an abstract idea and simply implementing it on a computer is not enough for a patent; there must be 'something more'. In Europe, the European Patent Convention excludes computer programs 'as such', but inventions involving software that produce a further technical effect, like controlling a machine more efficiently, may be patented. Many other countries are stricter. Arguments for software patents: they reward costly research and let small firms protect real innovations. Arguments against: software builds on many small ideas, patents can be vague, and 'patent trolls', companies that buy patents only to sue others, can tax innovation. As an engineer, you mostly need to know that patents exist, that they can affect your product, and that companies take them seriously.

Trademarks: A trademark is a sign that distinguishes the goods or services of one business from others: a name, logo, slogan, colour combination, or even a sound. Think of the names and logos of mobile operators, mobile banking services and food brands you see every day in Bangladesh. Trademarks protect consumers as well as companies: they tell you who made the product, so you can trust or avoid it. Unlike patents and copyright, a trademark can last indefinitely as long as it is used and renewed. Bangladesh's Trademarks Act 2009 governs registration through DPDT.

Trademark infringement: Infringement happens when someone uses an identical or confusingly similar mark for similar goods or services, so that customers could be misled. A shop selling phone covers branded with a big company's logo without permission infringes. So does an app called 'bKash Plus' that is not connected to the real company. Generic words cannot be owned as trademarks for the generic product: nobody can trademark 'Rice' for selling rice. That is why famous brands work hard to stop their names from becoming the generic word for a product.

Domain names and cybersquatting: Domain names are web addresses, and they often contain trademarks. Cybersquatting means registering a domain containing someone else's trademark in bad faith, hoping to sell it to them or to mislead users. ICANN, which coordinates internet domain names, adopted the Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy (UDRP) in 1999, giving trademark owners a faster way to recover such domains. Typo-squatting, registering misspellings of famous sites, is commonly used for phishing, which connects IP law to cyber crime (lesson 16).

Geographical indications: A geographical indication (GI) identifies a product as coming from a particular place whose qualities come from that place. Bangladesh has a law for GIs from 2013. Jamdani sari was registered as Bangladesh's first GI product in 2016, and Ilish (hilsa) soon after. GIs protect communities' traditional knowledge and help farmers and weavers earn more, an example of IP serving the public, not only corporations.

Trade secrets: A trade secret is business information that has commercial value because it is secret, and whose owner takes reasonable steps to keep it secret. Examples: a recipe, a manufacturing process, a customer list, the exact weights of a ranking algorithm, unreleased source code. Trade secrets need no registration and can last forever, but protection ends if the secret becomes public through legitimate means. Independent discovery and, in many places, reverse engineering of a legally bought product are generally allowed. What is forbidden is getting the secret by improper means: theft, bribery, hacking, or breaking a confidentiality duty.

Non-disclosure agreements: A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) is a contract in which one or both parties promise not to reveal confidential information. Employers, investors, clients and partners use NDAs constantly. A good NDA defines what is confidential, what is excluded (already public information, things you knew before), how long the duty lasts, and what happens at the end. Ethically, honour NDAs you sign; legally, remember that an NDA cannot force you to hide a crime.

Patent or trade secret? A worked choice: A Chattogram startup invents a new way to compress drone images that cuts file size by 40 percent. Option 1, patent it: public disclosure, 20 years of protection, costly filing in each country, and competitors learn the method. Option 2, keep it a trade secret: no cost to register, protection possibly forever, but if someone independently finds the method or reverse engineers the app, protection is gone. If the method can be seen by analysing the product, a patent is safer. If it runs hidden on the company's own servers, a trade secret may work better. Real companies make exactly this choice.

Industrial designs: An industrial design protects the visual appearance of a product: shape, pattern, lines, colours. Phone shapes, furniture, sari patterns and even graphical user interface icons in some countries can be registered as designs. Protection is shorter than patents in most systems and requires registration. A design protects only how the product looks, not how it works, so a phone's shape can be a design while its battery technology needs a patent.

An IP checklist for a new startup: Founders often ignore IP until a dispute arrives. A simple checklist avoids most trouble. First, search the name you want in the trademark database and app stores before printing anything, and register it if you can. Second, register the matching domain names, including common misspellings. Third, make sure every founder, employee and freelancer has signed an agreement that assigns the code and designs they create to the company. Fourth, keep a list of every third-party library, font and image with its licence (lesson 12). Fifth, mark confidential documents and use NDAs with partners. Sixth, before publicly presenting a genuinely new technical invention, think about whether to file a patent first, because public disclosure can destroy novelty. Each step takes hours; skipping them can cost years.

Real-life example 1, the clone app: A developer in Dhaka builds a ride-sharing app with exactly the same name style, logo colours and screen layout as a famous brand, but with his own code. Copyright on code is not infringed, since he wrote his own. But the confusingly similar name and logo can infringe the trademark, and a copied distinctive interface may raise design or copyright issues too. A unique name and branding avoids all of this.

Real-life example 2, the departing engineer: An engineer leaves a fintech company and joins a competitor, taking a copy of the fraud-detection rules on a USB stick. The rules are a trade secret protected by an NDA. Taking them is improper means, likely illegal, and unethical under ACM 1.7. Using his general skill in building fraud systems at the new company is fine. The line: skills go with you; secrets stay.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students mix up copyright, patent and trademark. Remember: copyright for creative expression including code, patent for inventions, trademark for brand identity. Others think patents are automatic; they must be applied for and granted. Some think trade secrets are illegal 'hiding'; they are legal and common. Exams ask: 'Compare copyright, patent, trademark and trade secret in a table', 'What are the requirements for a patent?', 'Discuss software patents', 'What is cybersquatting?', 'What should an NDA contain?'

Recap: Patents protect new, inventive, industrially applicable inventions for 20 years from filing in exchange for public disclosure, and must be applied for in each country. Software patents are limited and debated. Trademarks protect brand identity as long as used, and stop confusing marks; cybersquatting misuses them in domains. Geographical indications like Jamdani protect place-based products. Trade secrets protect valuable secret information while kept secret, often backed by NDAs. Designs protect appearance. Next lesson covers how software is licensed, including open source.
key_points: Patents protect new, inventive (non-obvious), industrially applicable inventions, in exchange for public disclosure.
Minimum patent term under TRIPS is 20 years from the filing date; patents are territorial and must be applied for.
Software patents are limited: the US Alice decision (2014) rejects abstract ideas just run on a computer; Europe excludes programs 'as such'.
Trademarks protect names, logos and other brand signs; they last as long as used and renewed, and stop confusingly similar marks.
Cybersquatting is registering domains with others' trademarks in bad faith; UDRP (1999) helps owners recover them.
Trade secrets protect valuable information while kept secret; independent discovery and reverse engineering are usually allowed, theft is not.
In Bangladesh, DPDT handles patents, designs and trademarks; Jamdani was the first registered geographical indication (2016).
lessons.tip: Make a 5-row comparison table (copyright, patent, trademark, trade secret, design) with columns: protects what, how obtained, how long, software example. It answers half of all IP exam questions.
lessons.task: Choose one product you own (phone, packaged snack, an app). Identify at least four kinds of IP that could protect different parts of it, and write one line for each explaining what is protected.

quiz.q: Which three requirements does a patent usually need?
quiz.explain: Patents need a new, non-obvious invention that can be used in industry.

quiz.q: A patent filed on 1 March 2010 with a 20-year term expires on...
options: The date it was granted plus 20 years
quiz.explain: The TRIPS minimum term counts 20 years from the filing date.

quiz.q: Registering 'bkash-offer-bd.com' in bad faith to mislead users is called...
quiz.explain: Cybersquatting is registering domains containing others' trademarks in bad faith.

quiz.q: Which statement about trade secrets is correct?
options: They must be registered with the government
They are protected only while kept secret, and theft is forbidden
Reverse engineering a legally bought product is always illegal
quiz.explain: Trade secrets need reasonable secrecy; improper means like theft are illegal, while independent discovery is generally allowed.

quiz.q: A clone app uses its own code but copies a famous brand's name style and logo. What is most likely infringed?
quiz.explain: A confusingly similar name and logo can mislead customers, which is trademark infringement.

lessons.title: Software Licensing and Open Source
lessons.content:
Imagine renting a flat in Dhanmondi. You get to live there, but the rental agreement says what you may and may not do: no subletting, no breaking walls, pay rent on the 5th. You do not own the building; you own permission to use it under conditions. Software works the same way. When you 'buy' an app, you almost never buy the code itself. You get a licence: a permission to use the software under certain conditions. And when you add an open source library to your project, you also accept a licence, with its own conditions. Ignoring these conditions is one of the most common legal mistakes developers make. This lesson explains how software licences work, the open source movement, and how to check your project's licences safely.

What a licence is: Because software is protected by copyright (lesson 10), nobody may copy, modify or distribute it without the owner's permission. A licence is that permission, usually with conditions. If you follow the conditions, you are a lawful user. If you break them, your permission may end, and you may be infringing copyright. A licence is not a sale of the copyright; the owner still owns the work.

Proprietary licences and EULAs: Proprietary software, like most commercial office suites, games and operating systems, is licensed under terms written by its owner, often called an End User License Agreement (EULA). Typical conditions: install on a limited number of devices, no reverse engineering, no copying, no renting, and a disclaimer of warranties. You usually accept by clicking 'I agree' (click-wrap, lesson 22). Source code is normally kept secret as a trade secret.

Licensing models: Proprietary software is sold in different ways. A perpetual licence lets you use a version forever after one payment. A subscription licence lets you use it only while you keep paying monthly or yearly, common for cloud software. Per-user, per-device and site licences count usage differently. Freeware is free to use but not free to modify; shareware can be tried free, then must be paid for. Free of charge does not mean free to copy or change.

Free software, the movement: In 1983 Richard Stallman launched the GNU project, and in 1985 he founded the Free Software Foundation. 'Free' here means freedom, not price: 'free as in free speech, not free beer'. The FSF defines four freedoms. Freedom 0: run the program for any purpose. Freedom 1: study how it works and change it, which requires access to source code. Freedom 2: redistribute copies. Freedom 3: distribute your modified versions. The ethical claim behind it: users should control the software they depend on, rather than software controlling users.

Open source: In 1998 the Open Source Initiative (OSI) was founded, using the term 'open source' to stress practical benefits for business: better quality through many reviewers, faster innovation, no vendor lock-in. The OSI's Open Source Definition requires, among other things, free redistribution, availability of source code, permission for derived works, and no discrimination against persons, groups or fields of use. In practice, most licences are both 'free' and 'open source'; the two names reflect different emphasis, ethics for one and practicality for the other. People often say FOSS (free and open source software) to include both.

Why open source matters to you: Almost every modern app depends on open source: the Linux kernel, Android's base, web servers, databases, programming languages and frameworks like Flutter, which is released under a BSD-style licence. A Bangladeshi startup can build a world-class product without paying for the base tools. But using open source responsibly means respecting each licence, and ideally contributing back fixes and improvements.

Permissive licences: Permissive licences let you do almost anything, including using the code in closed-source commercial products, with small conditions. MIT licence: keep the copyright notice and licence text in copies; that is nearly all. BSD licences (2-clause and 3-clause): similar to MIT; the 3-clause version also forbids using the authors' names to promote your product without permission. Apache License 2.0: like MIT but longer, with an explicit patent licence from contributors, a requirement to state significant changes, and to keep any NOTICE file. Apache 2.0 is popular with companies because of the patent clause.

Copyleft licences: Copyleft uses copyright to keep software free. The idea: you may use, change and share the code, but if you distribute a modified version or a program built on it, you must release it under the same licence with source code. The GNU General Public License (GPL), version 2 from 1991 and version 3 from 2007, is the best-known strong copyleft licence; the Linux kernel uses GPL version 2. The GNU Lesser GPL (LGPL) is weaker: you may link to an LGPL library from a proprietary program, as long as users can replace the library with a modified version. The GNU Affero GPL (AGPL) closes the 'server loophole': if users interact with your modified program over a network, you must offer them the source, even if you never distribute copies. The Mozilla Public License 2.0 is a file-level copyleft: changes to MPL files must be shared, but other files in your project can stay closed.

The distribution trigger: An important detail: the GPL's sharing duty is triggered by distribution, meaning giving copies to others. If you modify GPL software and use it only inside your company, you do not have to publish the changes. If you ship an app containing GPL code to users, you must provide the corresponding source under the GPL. The AGPL extends the trigger to network use. Many developers misunderstand this in both directions.

Licence compatibility: When you combine code under different licences, all the conditions must be satisfiable at once. MIT code can be included in a GPL project, because MIT's conditions fit inside the GPL's. GPL code cannot be included in a closed-source product you distribute, because the GPL requires the whole combined work to be GPL. Apache 2.0 code is considered compatible with GPL version 3 but not with GPL version 2, according to the Free Software Foundation. Tools and the SPDX standard identifiers (like 'MIT', 'Apache-2.0', 'GPL-3.0-only') help teams track licences automatically.

A worked dependency check: A Dhaka startup builds a closed-source Android app it will sell. Its dependency list: library A, MIT; library B, Apache-2.0; library C, BSD-3-Clause; library D, GPL-3.0; library E, LGPL-2.1, dynamically linked. Step 1, permissive ones (A, B, C): allowed; include their licence texts and notices in an 'Open source licences' screen. Step 2, E (LGPL): allowed if dynamically linked and users can replace it; check the specific conditions for mobile apps carefully. Step 3, D (GPL-3.0): shipping it inside a closed-source app would require releasing the whole app under the GPL. Options: replace D with a permissively licensed alternative, buy a commercial licence if the author offers dual licensing, or open-source the app. The team replaces D. Ten minutes of checking avoids a serious legal problem.

Dual licensing and open-core: Some projects offer the same code under two licences: GPL for free use, and a paid commercial licence for companies that want to keep their own code closed. Others use an open-core model: the core is open source, and extra enterprise features are proprietary. These are legitimate business models that fund open source development.

Contributing back, the ethical side: Open source runs on goodwill. Many critical libraries used by millions are maintained by one or two volunteers in their free time. Ethical use means more than obeying the licence: report bugs clearly, send fixes instead of only complaints, credit maintainers, and if your company earns money from a project, consider sponsoring it. When you contribute, you may be asked to sign a Contributor License Agreement (CLA) or confirm a Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO), which state that you have the right to submit the code. Only submit code you wrote or have rights to; copying your employer's code into a public project can break both your contract and copyright. Respect each project's code of conduct, too: open source communities are workplaces for many people.

Creative Commons: For non-software works, like images, music, text and datasets, Creative Commons licences are common. Elements: BY (give credit), SA (share alike: derivatives under the same licence), NC (non-commercial use only), ND (no derivatives). They combine, for example CC BY-SA. CC0 lets creators waive rights as far as the law allows, placing work close to the public domain. Wikipedia text is under CC BY-SA. For code, software licences like MIT or GPL are recommended instead of Creative Commons.

Piracy: Software piracy means copying, distributing or using software in violation of its licence, for example installing one licence on 50 office computers, or downloading cracked games. Common excuses: 'it's too expensive', 'big companies won't miss it', 'everyone does it'. Ethically it takes value without the creator's consent, and it hurts local developers most: a Bangladeshi accounting software company loses sales when its product is pirated. Practically, cracked software often carries malware. Better options: free student licences, free and open source alternatives, regional pricing, and subscription plans.

Real-life example 1, the freelance delivery: A Bangladeshi freelancer delivers a website to a foreign client, quietly including a GPL plugin modified with client-specific code. The client later sells the site as a closed product to others. Because distribution happened, GPL obligations apply. The freelancer should have told the client about the licence at the start. Honest licence disclosure is part of professional service.

Real-life example 2, the university lab: A university lab in Rajshahi has 40 computers but only 5 licences for a commercial design tool, installed on all 40. An audit by the vendor could lead to large fines and embarrassment. The lab switches to an open source alternative for teaching and keeps the 5 licensed copies for research that needs them. Respecting licences and saving money can go together.

Common mistakes and exam points: 'Open source means no rules.' No, every licence has conditions. 'GPL means I can't use it commercially.' No, you can sell GPL software; you must share source with recipients. 'Free means free of charge.' In 'free software' it means freedom. Exams ask: 'Compare permissive and copyleft licences', 'State the four freedoms', 'What is the difference between GPL, LGPL and AGPL?', 'Explain licence compatibility with an example', 'Discuss the ethics of software piracy'.

Recap: A licence is permission to use copyrighted software under conditions. Proprietary licences (EULAs) restrict copying and hide source; licensing models include perpetual, subscription and per-user. Free software stresses four freedoms; open source stresses practical benefits. Permissive licences (MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0) allow closed use with notice; copyleft licences (GPL, LGPL, AGPL, MPL) require sharing on distribution or network use. Check compatibility of every dependency. Creative Commons covers non-software works. Piracy breaks licences and hurts local creators. Next we move to privacy, starting with what privacy is and why it matters.
key_points: A software licence is permission to use copyrighted software under conditions; buying an app usually buys a licence, not the code.
Proprietary EULAs typically restrict installs, copying and reverse engineering; models include perpetual, subscription and per-user.
The FSF's four freedoms: run, study and change, redistribute, distribute modified versions; 'free' means freedom, not price.
Permissive licences (MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0) allow use in closed products if you keep notices; Apache 2.0 adds a patent grant.
Copyleft (GPL) requires distributed derivatives to be released under the same licence with source; LGPL is weaker, AGPL covers network use.
Always check licence compatibility of dependencies; a GPL library in a closed app you distribute is a serious problem.
Creative Commons (BY, SA, NC, ND, CC0) is for non-software works; piracy violates licences and often spreads malware.
lessons.tip: In every project, keep a LICENSES.md or use your package manager's licence report. Check new dependencies' licences before you add them, not the night before release.
lessons.task: Open any Flutter, Node or Python project you have and list every direct dependency with its licence (pub.dev, npm and PyPI show it). Mark each as permissive or copyleft, and decide whether the app could be sold as closed source.

quiz.q: What does 'free' mean in 'free software' according to the FSF?
options: Freedom to run, study, change and share
quiz.explain: It is 'free as in free speech, not free beer': the four freedoms.

quiz.q: Which licence lets you use the code in a closed-source product as long as you keep the copyright notice?
quiz.explain: MIT is permissive: keep the notice and licence text, and closed use is allowed.

quiz.q: When is the GPL's duty to share source usually triggered?
options: When you distribute the software or a derivative to others
When you read the source code
When you use it privately inside your company only
quiz.explain: The GPL's obligations apply on distribution; AGPL extends this to network use.

quiz.q: A closed-source app you will sell includes a GPL-3.0 library. What is a correct fix?
options: Ignore it if the app is small
Replace it with a permissively licensed alternative or get a commercial licence
quiz.explain: Otherwise the whole app would need to be released under the GPL.

quiz.q: Which licence is designed to close the 'server loophole'?
quiz.explain: The Affero GPL requires offering source to users who interact with modified software over a network.

lessons.title: Privacy Foundations: What Privacy Is and Why It Matters
lessons.content:
Imagine someone follows you all day with a notebook. They write down which shop you visited, who you called, what you searched, which medicine you bought, which posts you liked, and where you slept. They never hurt you. They just write. Would you feel free? Most people would feel uneasy, even if they had done nothing wrong. Today, that notebook exists, spread across phones, apps, cameras and servers. This lesson asks what privacy really is, why it matters even for people with 'nothing to hide', and how data that looks anonymous can still point straight at you.

What privacy is: Privacy is hard to define in one line, so thinkers have offered several views. In 1890, two American lawyers, Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis, wrote a famous article called 'The Right to Privacy', worried about new portable cameras and gossip newspapers. They described privacy as 'the right to be let alone'. In 1967 Alan Westin defined privacy as the claim of individuals to decide for themselves when, how and to what extent information about them is communicated to others. Today we often speak of informational privacy: control over personal information.

Three kinds of privacy: It helps to split privacy into types. Physical or territorial privacy: your body and your space, like your room or your bag. Decisional privacy: making personal choices, such as religion or medical treatment, without interference. Informational privacy: control over data about you, such as your phone number, location, health records, messages and browsing history. Computing mostly affects the third type, but cameras and smart devices reach into the first as well.

Privacy as a right: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948, Article 12, says no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with their privacy, family, home or correspondence. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights repeats this in Article 17. The Constitution of Bangladesh, in Article 43, protects citizens' right to privacy of correspondence and other means of communication, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law for things like security and public order. So privacy is not just a preference; it is recognised as a human right, though never an unlimited one.

Why privacy matters, five reasons: First, freedom and dignity: people behave differently when watched, and constant watching makes people timid. Second, protection from harm: exposed data can lead to fraud, stalking, blackmail, discrimination and violence. Third, relationships: we share different things with doctors, friends and employers; privacy lets us keep those circles separate. Fourth, power balance: whoever holds detailed data about you can influence you, by targeted advertising, price discrimination or political manipulation. Fifth, democracy: journalists, activists and voters need room to think, talk and organise without fear.

Privacy versus security: The two words are often mixed up. Security is about protecting data and systems from unauthorised access: locks, passwords, encryption, firewalls (deep-cse-6-2). Privacy is about whether personal data should be collected, used and shared at all, and on what terms. A company can have excellent security and still violate privacy, for example by collecting far more data than needed and selling it to partners through perfectly secure channels. And weak security almost always causes privacy harm, because a breach exposes personal data. Good engineers need both: decide carefully what to collect, then protect it well.

The 'nothing to hide' argument: A common reply is: 'I have nothing to hide, so why should I care?' Legal scholar Daniel Solove and others have answered this carefully. Privacy is not only about hiding wrongdoing. Everyone has things they keep private for good reasons: a health condition, salary, a family dispute, a political opinion, a location they visit. Data can be misread or wrong: an innocent search history can look suspicious out of context. Rules change: something harmless today may be punished tomorrow. And the question can be turned around: if you have nothing to hide, would you hand your unlocked phone to a stranger for an hour? Most people would not.

Contextual integrity: Philosopher Helen Nissenbaum suggested a useful way to judge privacy problems, called contextual integrity. Information flows always happen inside a context with its own norms. Your medical test result flowing from you to your doctor fits the norms of healthcare. The same result flowing from a lab to your employer breaks those norms. The question is not 'is this data public or private?' but 'does this flow match the expectations of the context where it was shared?' This explains why people get upset when a photo shared with friends is reposted publicly, even though it was never secret.

Surveillance: Surveillance means systematic watching of people, by governments, companies or individuals. Government surveillance can protect security but can also chill speech and target critics. Workplace surveillance monitors employees' screens, keystrokes or locations. Commercial surveillance tracks consumers across apps and websites, often through cookies, software development kits inside apps, device identifiers and location data. Philosopher Jeremy Bentham designed a prison called the panopticon, where a guard could watch any prisoner without being seen, so prisoners behaved as if always watched. Many writers use the panopticon to describe modern digital surveillance.

Data brokers and profiling: Data brokers are companies that collect personal data from many sources, such as public records, loyalty cards, apps and websites, combine it into profiles, and sell or rent those profiles. A profile might guess your income, health interests, religion or whether you are pregnant. Profiling means using data to predict characteristics or behaviour. It can be useful, for example fraud detection, but it can also be unfair or invasive, especially when people do not know it is happening and cannot correct mistakes.

The privacy paradox: Surveys repeatedly find that people say they care deeply about privacy, yet they install apps that request every permission and click 'accept all cookies' without reading. This gap is called the privacy paradox. It does not mean people are lying. Privacy policies are long and hard to read, choices are designed to be tiring, the harms are delayed and invisible, and often there is no real alternative app to use. This is why many experts argue that privacy cannot be left to individual choices alone; it needs good laws and good default designs by engineers, which is exactly where the next two lessons go.

Metadata: Metadata is data about data: who called whom, when, for how long, from which tower; or when a photo was taken and with what GPS coordinates. People often think metadata is harmless because it does not contain the message content. But patterns reveal a lot. Calls to a cancer clinic, then to a life-insurance office, then to a lawyer, tell a story without any words. A photo's hidden GPS tags can reveal your home address. Many apps strip location from photos when posting, but not all do.

Anonymisation and re-identification: Companies often say data is safe because it is 'anonymised': names and phone numbers removed. But remaining fields can act as quasi-identifiers that, combined, point to one person. In a famous 2000 study, computer scientist Latanya Sweeney estimated that about 87 percent of the US population could be uniquely identified using just ZIP code, gender and date of birth. Earlier, she had identified a state governor's hospital records in a supposedly anonymous dataset by matching those three fields with a public voter list.

Why re-identification is so easy, worked: Consider a small area with 20,000 people. Suppose birthdays spread over about 80 years of possible dates, roughly 365 x 80 = 29,200 dates, and there are 2 recorded genders. That gives 29,200 x 2 = 58,400 possible combinations of birth date and gender. On average there are only 20,000 / 58,400, about 0.34 people per combination. The chance that a given person shares their exact combination with nobody else is about 71 percent. So in this area, knowing just birth date, gender and the area code identifies most people uniquely. Add a profession or a car model and almost everyone becomes unique.

More famous cases: In 2006 AOL released about 20 million search queries from roughly 650,000 users for research, replacing names with numbers. Journalists quickly identified some users from their searches about their neighbourhoods and names. Also in 2006, Netflix released anonymised movie ratings for a competition; researchers Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov showed that many users could be re-identified by matching a few ratings and dates with public reviews on another website. Lesson: removing names is not anonymisation.

k-anonymity: One classic defence, also proposed by Sweeney, is k-anonymity. A dataset is k-anonymous if every record is identical to at least k minus 1 other records on its quasi-identifiers. Techniques: generalisation, such as replacing exact age 23 with the range 20 to 29, or a full postcode with its first digits; and suppression, removing rare records. Worked example: a hospital table has rows (age 23, area 1207, female), (age 27, area 1209, female), (age 25, area 1205, female). Generalise to (20 to 29, area 120*, female) and all three rows look the same, so this group is 3-anonymous. Limits: if all three share the same diagnosis, an attacker still learns it. Lesson 15 covers stronger ideas, like differential privacy.

Real-life example 1, the leaked NID database: Suppose a government service's database exposes citizens' names, national ID numbers, phone numbers, addresses and photos. Even without bank details, criminals can use such data for SIM-swap fraud, fake loans and convincing phishing calls ('Sir, I am calling from your bank, your NID number is...'). Each piece looks small; together they are a toolkit for crime. Protecting data is protecting people.

Real-life example 2, the fitness app map: A fitness app publishes a global heat map of users' running routes, made from 'anonymous' aggregated data. In remote areas, the few glowing paths can reveal secret locations such as private compounds or security sites, because the only people running there are staff. Aggregated data can still leak sensitive patterns. Something similar really happened with a popular fitness app's map in 2018.

Common mistakes and exam points: 'Anonymised data is safe.' Not without careful analysis. 'Public data has no privacy issues.' Contextual integrity says flows still matter. 'Privacy only matters for criminals.' It matters for everyone. Exams ask: 'Define privacy and give its types', 'Explain why privacy is important', 'Discuss the nothing-to-hide argument', 'What is re-identification? Give an example', 'Explain k-anonymity with a table'.

Recap: Privacy is the right to be let alone and to control information about yourself, in physical, decisional and informational forms, recognised in human rights law and Bangladesh's Constitution. It protects freedom, safety, relationships, power balance and democracy. Contextual integrity judges flows by the norms of their context. Surveillance, data brokers and metadata reveal far more than people expect. Removing names does not anonymise: quasi-identifiers like birth date, gender and area can re-identify most people, as Sweeney, AOL and Netflix showed. k-anonymity helps but has limits. Next lesson covers the laws that protect personal data.
key_points: Privacy: 'the right to be let alone' (Warren and Brandeis, 1890) and control over information about yourself (Westin, 1967).
Types: physical, decisional and informational privacy; computing mostly affects informational privacy.
Privacy is recognised in UDHR Article 12, ICCPR Article 17, and Article 43 of the Bangladesh Constitution (correspondence and communication).
The 'nothing to hide' argument fails: everyone has legitimate secrets, data can be misread, and rules change.
Contextual integrity (Nissenbaum): judge an information flow by the norms of the context where it was shared.
Removing names is not anonymisation; quasi-identifiers like birth date, gender and postcode can re-identify most people (Sweeney: about 87% in the US).
k-anonymity makes each record identical to at least k-1 others on quasi-identifiers, using generalisation and suppression, but still leaks shared sensitive values.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a dataset, ask: 'Which columns, combined, could point to one person?' Training this reflex now will save you from leaking data later.
lessons.task: Look at the details of 5 photos on your phone (Info or Details). Note which ones have GPS location, date and device model. Then check your camera and gallery settings to see whether location tagging can be turned off.

quiz.q: Who described privacy as 'the right to be let alone'?
quiz.explain: Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis wrote 'The Right to Privacy' in 1890.

quiz.q: Which article of the Bangladesh Constitution protects privacy of correspondence and communication?
quiz.explain: Article 43 protects privacy of correspondence and other means of communication, subject to reasonable legal restrictions.

quiz.q: With 58,400 possible birth-date and gender combinations and 20,000 people, about how many people share each combination on average?
quiz.explain: 20,000 / 58,400 is about 0.34, so most combinations hold zero or one person.

quiz.q: Contextual integrity says a privacy problem occurs when...
options: Any data is stored on a computer
An information flow breaks the norms of the context where it was shared
A user has something illegal to hide
quiz.explain: Nissenbaum's framework judges flows against the expectations of their original context.

quiz.q: In a 3-anonymous table, each record...
options: Matches at least 2 other records on its quasi-identifiers
Has its name replaced with 3 stars
