lessons.title: Data Protection Law: Principles, GDPR and Beyond
lessons.content:
Think about the rules for a bank locker. The bank may only open it with your key, must keep it safe, must tell you if it was broken into, and must give it back when you close the account. Nobody expects the bank to just 'try its best'. There are rules. Data protection law does the same for your personal data held by companies and governments: it sets rules for why data may be collected, how it must be kept, what rights you have, and what happens when rules are broken. This lesson explains the core principles that most data protection laws share, the European GDPR as the most influential example, and the situation in Bangladesh, kept version-neutral because laws in this area are changing.

What personal data is: Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable living person. Obvious examples: name, phone number, NID number, email, photo. Less obvious: IP address, device ID, location history, cookie identifiers, voice recordings, and combinations of fields that can single someone out (lesson 13). Many laws define special or sensitive categories needing extra protection, such as health, biometrics, religion, political opinion, ethnicity and sex life.

Key roles: Laws usually name three roles. The data subject is the person the data is about. The controller decides why and how the data is processed, for example a ride-sharing company. The processor processes data on the controller's behalf, for example the cloud provider storing the company's database or an SMS gateway sending messages. Controllers carry the main responsibility, but processors have duties too.

The roots, fair information practices: Modern data protection grew from 'fair information practice' principles in the 1970s. In 1980 the OECD published Privacy Guidelines with eight principles: collection limitation, data quality, purpose specification, use limitation, security safeguards, openness, individual participation and accountability. These ideas appear, in different words, in almost every data protection law since. If you remember them, you understand the skeleton of every law.

The GDPR: The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) was adopted in 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018. It is important even outside Europe for two reasons. First, its territorial scope: it applies to organisations anywhere in the world that offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour. A Bangladeshi software company building an app for European customers may have to follow it. Second, many countries have used it as a model for their own laws.

GDPR's seven principles: Article 5 says personal data must be: processed lawfully, fairly and transparently; collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not used in incompatible ways (purpose limitation); adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary (data minimisation); accurate and kept up to date; kept no longer than necessary (storage limitation); processed securely (integrity and confidentiality); and the controller must be able to demonstrate compliance (accountability). Notice how close these are to the OECD list.

Lawful bases: Under GDPR you need one of six lawful bases to process personal data: consent of the person; necessity for a contract with them (for example, using an address to deliver an order); a legal obligation (for example, keeping tax records); protecting someone's vital interests (a medical emergency); a public task performed by an authority; or legitimate interests of the controller, balanced against the person's rights (for example, basic fraud prevention). A common mistake is to think consent is always required. It is one basis among six, and often not the best one.

Valid consent: When consent is used, it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action. Pre-ticked boxes do not count. Silence does not count. Consent bundled with unrelated terms ('agree to marketing or you cannot use the app') is usually not freely given. People must be able to withdraw consent as easily as they gave it. For children's data in online services, parental consent is required below an age that each EU country sets between 13 and 16.

Data subject rights: GDPR gives people rights including: the right to be informed (clear privacy notices); the right of access (get a copy of your data); the right to rectification (correct wrong data); the right to erasure, often called the right to be forgotten, in certain situations; the right to restrict processing; the right to data portability (receive your data in a machine-readable format to move it elsewhere); the right to object, including to direct marketing at any time; and rights related to automated decision-making, including the right not to be subject to certain decisions based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects. Controllers must usually respond within one month.

Breach notification: A personal data breach is a security incident leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, change, disclosure of or access to personal data. Under GDPR, the controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to risk people's rights. If the risk to people is high, they must also be told directly. Worked timing: a breach is discovered on Monday at 10:00. The 72-hour window ends on Thursday at 10:00. Engineers help by keeping logs that show what was accessed, which is what makes a fast, accurate report possible.

Other duties: GDPR also requires data protection by design and by default (lesson 15), records of processing activities, data protection impact assessments (DPIAs) for high-risk processing, contracts with processors, appointing a data protection officer in some cases, and rules for transferring data outside the EU only where protection stays adequate.

Cross-border transfers and data localisation: Data moves across borders constantly: an app in Sylhet may store data on servers in Singapore and send emails through a service in the United States. Data protection laws worry that protection could disappear once data leaves the country. GDPR allows transfers outside the EU only to countries judged adequate, or with safeguards such as standard contractual clauses. Some countries go further with data localisation rules that require certain data, often financial, health or government data, to be stored inside the country. Supporters say this protects citizens and helps local investigation; critics say it raises costs, can weaken security, and may make government surveillance easier. As an engineer, always know where your data physically lives and which law follows it there.

Fines, worked: GDPR fines for the most serious violations can reach up to 20 million euros or 4 percent of the company's total worldwide annual turnover of the previous year, whichever is higher. A lower tier goes up to 10 million euros or 2 percent. Worked example: a company with a turnover of 2 billion euros: 4 percent is 80 million euros, which is higher than 20 million, so the maximum is 80 million. A company with a turnover of 100 million euros: 4 percent is 4 million, lower than 20 million, so the maximum is 20 million. These are maximums; real fines depend on seriousness, intent and cooperation. Large fines have been imposed on major technology companies.

Other laws around the world: Many countries now have comprehensive data protection laws. India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in 2023. Brazil has the LGPD, and many countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America have their own. The United States has no single general federal privacy law but has sector laws, such as HIPAA for health and COPPA for children's data online, plus state laws like California's. The pattern worldwide is clear: data protection is becoming normal business law.

Bangladesh, version-neutral: Bangladesh's Constitution protects privacy of correspondence and communication (Article 43). For a long time the country had no single comprehensive personal data protection law; protections were scattered across sector rules, such as banking secrecy and telecom rules, and cyber laws that made it an offence to collect or use someone's identity information without lawful authority. In recent years the government has worked on a dedicated personal data protection law through several drafts, with debate about data localisation (keeping data inside the country), the powers of the regulator, and government access to data. Because this area is changing, always check the current law and official guidance before advising on compliance. Good engineering practice, following the principles in this lesson, prepares you for whatever final form the law takes.

A practical checklist for engineers: For every new feature that touches personal data, ask eight questions. What exact data do we collect? Why, and under which lawful basis? Is every field necessary? Who can access it inside the company? Which processors or third parties receive it? Where is it stored, and in which country? How long do we keep it, and how is it deleted? How would we detect and report a breach? Writing the answers in the design document takes half an hour, and it turns legal principles into concrete engineering decisions that reviewers can check.

Real-life example 1, a Bangladeshi app with European users: A Dhaka company runs a Bangla language learning app with many users in Europe. Under GDPR's scope rules, it likely must comply for those users. Practical steps: a clear privacy notice, a lawful basis for each use (contract for lessons, consent for marketing emails), a way to download and delete accounts, a processor agreement with the cloud host, a breach response plan with the 72-hour clock, and minimal analytics. These steps also make the app better for Bangladeshi users.

Real-life example 2, the hospital SMS: A private hospital in Khulna sends test-result notifications by SMS, including the test name, such as 'Your HIV test result is ready', to phones that family members often share. Health data is a special category. A safer design: send only 'Your report is ready; log in with your PIN', and show the details in a protected portal. Same service, much less risk.

Common mistakes and exam points: 'Consent is always needed.' No, there are six lawful bases. 'GDPR only matters in Europe.' Its scope reaches organisations worldwide that target or monitor people in the EU. 'Anonymised data is personal data.' Truly anonymous data is outside GDPR, but pseudonymised data is still personal data. Exams ask: 'State the GDPR principles', 'List the lawful bases', 'Explain data subject rights', 'What are the breach notification rules?', 'Compute the maximum fine for a given turnover', 'Discuss data protection in Bangladesh'.

Recap: Personal data is information about an identifiable person, with special categories needing more care. Controllers decide, processors act for them. The OECD's eight principles became the skeleton of modern laws. GDPR (applying since 25 May 2018) has seven principles, six lawful bases, strict consent rules, strong individual rights, 72-hour breach notice and fines up to 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide turnover. Other countries, including India, have similar laws. Bangladesh protects communication privacy constitutionally and has been developing a dedicated law; check the current version. Next lesson turns principles into engineering practice.
key_points: Personal data is any information about an identified or identifiable person; special categories (health, biometrics, religion and more) need extra care.
Roles: data subject, controller (decides why and how) and processor (acts for the controller).
OECD 1980 principles: collection limitation, data quality, purpose specification, use limitation, security, openness, individual participation, accountability.
GDPR (applies since 25 May 2018) principles: lawfulness and transparency, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security, accountability.
Six lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests; valid consent is free, specific, informed, unambiguous and withdrawable.
Rights include access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection and protections against solely automated decisions; breaches go to the regulator within 72 hours where feasible.
Maximum GDPR fine: 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher; Bangladesh's dedicated law has been developing, so check the current version.
lessons.tip: Memorise GDPR through the OECD list: if you know the eight fair information principles, you can rebuild GDPR's seven principles and explain most of its duties in your own words.

quiz.explain: The six bases are consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests.

72 hours of becoming aware, where feasible

quiz.explain: The processor acts on behalf of the controller, who decides why and how data is processed.

Agreeing to marketing as a condition for using an unrelated service

lessons.title: Privacy Engineering: Building Privacy into Software
lessons.content:
Imagine building a house and only remembering the doors and locks after the family has moved in. You would have to break walls, the result would look patched, and it would never be as safe as a house designed with doors from the start. Privacy in software is the same. Adding it after launch, when the database already holds millions of unnecessary records, is expensive and weak. Privacy engineering means designing privacy into systems from the first sketch. This lesson turns the principles and laws from lessons 13 and 14 into concrete techniques you can use in your next project.

Privacy by design: The idea was popularised by Ann Cavoukian, then Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, Canada, who described seven foundational principles. One, proactive not reactive: prevent privacy problems instead of fixing them after harm. Two, privacy as the default setting: users are protected without having to do anything. Three, privacy embedded into design: part of the architecture, not an add-on. Four, full functionality: aim for win-win, not a false trade-off between privacy and features. Five, end-to-end security: protect data through its whole life, from collection to deletion. Six, visibility and transparency: people can check what happens. Seven, respect for user privacy: keep the user at the centre. GDPR later turned this into a legal duty called data protection by design and by default.

Step 1, build a data inventory: You cannot protect what you do not know you have. A data inventory, sometimes called a data map, lists every personal data field the system touches: what it is, why it is collected, where it is stored, who can access it, which third parties receive it, and how long it is kept. A simple spreadsheet is enough for a small team. Many breaches involve forgotten copies: old backups, test databases filled with real customer data, log files full of phone numbers.

Step 2, data minimisation in practice: For each field, ask: does this feature truly need it? A food delivery app needs a delivery address, but does it need date of birth? Probably not; if age matters for some items, a yes or no 'over 18' answer may be enough. Location for a delivery is needed while delivering, but continuous background location when the app is closed usually is not. Choose coarse data over precise data when possible: city instead of exact GPS, age range instead of birth date. Every field you do not collect is a field that can never leak.

Step 3, purpose limitation in code: Purpose limitation means data collected for one reason is not quietly reused for another. In code, this can be supported by tagging data with its purpose, separating databases by purpose, and requiring review before any new use. Example: phone numbers collected for login one-time passwords should not flow automatically into the marketing system. A simple access rule, where the marketing service has no permission to read the authentication table, enforces this technically.

Step 4, pseudonymisation versus anonymisation: Pseudonymisation replaces direct identifiers with artificial ones, such as replacing a customer's phone number with a random customer ID, while keeping a separate, protected table that links them. It reduces risk, but the data is still personal data because it can be linked back. Anonymisation means the data can no longer be linked to a person by any reasonably likely means, which is much harder to achieve (lesson 13). Analysts can often work with pseudonymised data without ever seeing names.

Why plain hashing of phone numbers fails, worked: A team 'anonymises' phone numbers by storing SHA-256 hashes. But Bangladeshi mobile numbers have a known shape: '01', then an operator digit, then 8 more digits. If the operator digit can be one of 7 values, there are only 7 x 10^8 = 700,000,000 possible numbers. A normal computer can compute millions of hashes per second; at 10 million per second, hashing every possible number takes about 700,000,000 / 10,000,000 = 70 seconds, producing a lookup table that reverses every hash. Fixes: use a keyed hash (HMAC) with a secret key stored separately, or random IDs with a protected mapping table. Small input spaces make simple hashes reversible.

Step 5, security across the life cycle: Privacy depends on security (deep-cse-6-2). Encrypt data in transit with TLS and at rest with disk or database encryption. Store passwords with slow, salted password hashing functions designed for that purpose, never plain text or fast hashes. Apply least privilege: each person and service gets only the access it needs. Log access to sensitive data and review the logs. Keep secrets out of source code. Patch dependencies. And make test environments use synthetic or properly masked data, not production copies.

Step 6, retention and deletion: Storage limitation means deleting data when it is no longer needed. Engineering techniques: set a retention period for each data type in the inventory; run scheduled jobs that delete or anonymise expired records; make sure deletion also covers backups after their rotation period, caches, search indexes and analytics copies; and implement account deletion that really deletes, not just hides. Worked example: a ride app keeps exact trip GPS traces for 90 days for disputes and safety, then keeps only city-level trip summaries. If 200,000 trips happen per day, the system never stores more than about 200,000 x 90 = 18,000,000 detailed traces instead of growing forever.

Logs, analytics and third-party SDKs: Some of the biggest privacy leaks happen in places developers forget. Debug logs often print full request bodies, including phone numbers, OTP codes and addresses, and those logs are kept for months and read by many people. Mask sensitive fields before logging, for example showing only the last 3 digits of a phone number. Analytics tools should receive event counts, not names. Third-party SDKs for ads, crash reporting or social login can collect data on their own once you add them to your app, so read what each SDK collects, turn off what you do not need, and list it in your privacy notice. You are responsible for what the code you ship does, even if someone else wrote it.

Step 7, consent and transparency design: When consent is the lawful basis, the interface matters. Good patterns: ask at the moment the permission is needed, with a short reason ('Allow location so the rider can find you'); make 'Allow' and 'Don't allow' equally easy; give separate choices for separate purposes; and provide a privacy dashboard where users can see and change choices later. Privacy notices should be layered: a short, plain summary first, with details available for those who want them, in Bangla as well as English for Bangladeshi users.

Dark patterns: Dark patterns are interface designs that trick users into choices they would not otherwise make. The term was coined by designer Harry Brignull in 2010. Examples: confirmshaming ('No thanks, I don't care about saving money'); the roach motel, easy to sign up and very hard to cancel; pre-checked boxes that share data; hiding the 'reject all' button behind several screens while 'accept all' is bright and big; sneaking items into a shopping basket; and forced continuity, where a free trial silently turns into a paid subscription. Dark patterns violate the ACM Code's honesty principle and often data protection and consumer laws. Human Computer Interaction (deep-cse-5-5) covers design techniques in more depth.

Step 8, data protection impact assessment: For high-risk processing, such as large-scale health data, biometrics, monitoring public spaces or profiling with significant effects, GDPR requires a DPIA, and it is good practice anywhere. Steps: describe the processing and its purposes; assess necessity and proportionality; identify risks to people, such as discrimination, fraud or exposure; and plan measures to reduce them. Doing it before building is far cheaper than redesigning after a complaint.

Differential privacy, the idea: Sometimes we want useful statistics about a group without revealing anything about any individual. Differential privacy, introduced by Cynthia Dwork and colleagues in 2006, gives a mathematical guarantee: adding or removing any one person's data changes the output only a little, so the output reveals almost nothing about that person. It works by adding carefully calibrated random noise. The amount of protection is controlled by a parameter called epsilon: smaller epsilon means more noise and more privacy, but less accuracy. It has been used, for example, by the US Census Bureau for 2020 census products and by large technology companies for usage statistics.

Randomised response, a worked example: An old survey trick shows the core idea. You want to know what fraction of students have copied an assignment, but nobody will answer honestly. Rule: each student flips a coin secretly. Heads: answer truthfully. Tails: flip again and answer 'yes' for heads, 'no' for tails. Any single 'yes' could be just the coin, so each student has deniability. But the group statistic can be recovered. If the true fraction is p, the expected fraction of 'yes' answers is 0.5 x p + 0.25. If 35 percent answer 'yes', then 0.35 = 0.5p + 0.25, so p = 2 x (0.35 minus 0.25) = 0.20, about 20 percent. Privacy for each person, useful truth for the group.

Real-life example 1, redesigning a Dhaka clinic booking app: The first version asked for full name, NID number, date of birth, address, phone, email and symptoms, and stored everything forever. A privacy-engineered redesign: phone number and name only for booking; symptoms optional and visible only to the doctor; NID only where legally required for specific tests; data encrypted; appointments older than two years reduced to anonymous counts; a 'delete my account' button. Bookings still work. The risk drops dramatically.

Real-life example 2, the contact-tracing debate: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries built contact-tracing apps. Some designs stored everyone's location centrally. Others, using a decentralised Bluetooth approach, kept proximity records on phones and shared only random rotating identifiers, so no central server knew who met whom. The second approach shows privacy by design in action: the public health goal could be pursued while collecting far less personal data.

Common mistakes and exam points: 'Hashing makes data anonymous.' Not for small input spaces like phone numbers. 'Privacy can be added later.' It becomes expensive and weak. 'More data is always better for the business.' More data means more risk, cost and legal duty. Exams ask: 'State the seven principles of privacy by design', 'Distinguish pseudonymisation from anonymisation', 'What are dark patterns? Give examples', 'Explain differential privacy and randomised response', 'Describe the steps of a DPIA'.

Recap: Privacy by design (Cavoukian's seven principles) means proactive, default, embedded, positive-sum, end-to-end, transparent, user-centred privacy. In practice: build a data inventory, minimise fields, enforce purpose limits in code, pseudonymise carefully (plain hashes of phone numbers can be reversed in about a minute), secure the whole life cycle, set retention and real deletion, design honest consent, avoid dark patterns, run DPIAs for risky processing, and use differential privacy for safe statistics. Next we turn to the darker side of computing: computer crime.
key_points: Privacy by design (Cavoukian): proactive, privacy by default, embedded, full functionality, end-to-end security, transparency, respect for users.
Start with a data inventory: every personal field, its purpose, location, access, recipients and retention.
Minimise data: collect only what each feature truly needs, and prefer coarse data (age range, city) over precise data.
Pseudonymised data is still personal data; plain hashes of phone numbers can be reversed quickly because the input space is small, so use keyed hashes or random IDs.
Set retention periods and real deletion, including backups, caches, logs and analytics copies.
Dark patterns (confirmshaming, roach motel, pre-checked boxes, hidden reject buttons) trick users and break honesty and often the law.
Differential privacy adds calibrated noise so outputs reveal almost nothing about any individual; randomised response is a simple example.
lessons.tip: Before writing any database schema, write a one-line purpose next to every column containing personal data. If you cannot write the purpose, delete the column.
lessons.task: Simulate randomised response with 20 friends or classmates on a harmless yes/no question. Count the 'yes' answers, compute p = 2 x (fraction yes - 0.25), and compare with what you would expect.

The number of possible phone numbers is small enough to hash them all and build a lookup table

Making it easy to subscribe but very hard to cancel is a dark pattern called...

It is still personal data because it can be linked back to people
It cannot be used for analytics

lessons.title: Computer Crime: Types, Criminals and Famous Cases
lessons.content:
A pickpocket on a crowded bus in Gulistan can steal one wallet at a time, and he must be physically there. A cyber criminal sitting in another country can try a million wallets in an hour, never touch anyone, and disappear before anyone notices. Crime itself is old; what computers change is scale, distance, speed and how hard it is to catch the criminal. This lesson describes the main types of computer crime, who commits them and why, and several famous cases, including one that hit Bangladesh directly. The technical details of attacks belong to Computer Security & Cryptography (deep-cse-6-2) and Advanced Cyber Security (deep-cse-9-5); here we focus on what makes them crimes and the harm they cause.

What computer crime is: Computer crime, or cybercrime, means illegal acts in which computers or networks are the target, the tool, or the place where evidence is stored. Laws differ between countries, but most recognise three broad groups. Crimes against computers and data: breaking into systems, damaging data, spreading malware, disrupting services. Crimes using computers: fraud, theft, forgery, extortion and identity theft done through digital means. Content-related crimes: illegal content such as child sexual abuse material, and in many countries harassment, threats or certain kinds of hateful or defamatory content. Intellectual property crimes like large-scale piracy are often added as a fourth group.

Unauthorised access: Unauthorised access, often called hacking in everyday speech, means entering a computer system, account or data without permission, or going beyond the permission you have. Guessing a classmate's password, logging into an ex-employer's server with an old account, or reading files you were not allowed to open all count, even if you change nothing. Almost every cyber law makes this an offence, because access is the first step of most other crimes. 'I just wanted to see if I could' is not a defence.

Malware: Malware is malicious software. Viruses attach to other programs and spread when those run. Worms spread by themselves across networks. Trojans pretend to be useful software while doing harm. Spyware secretly collects information. Keyloggers record what you type. Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment. Botnets are networks of infected devices controlled by a criminal. Writing malware for research in a lab is not itself the same as spreading it; laws generally target creating or distributing it with intent to cause harm or unauthorised access.

Ransomware: Ransomware has become one of the most damaging crimes. The criminal gets in, often through phishing or an unpatched server, encrypts the victim's files, and demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, for the decryption key. Modern gangs also steal data first and threaten to publish it, called double extortion. Hospitals, local governments and companies have been shut down for days. Paying does not guarantee recovery and funds more crime. Good backups kept offline are the most important defence, together with quick patching, multi-factor authentication and a rehearsed recovery plan. An organisation that has tested restoring its data from backup can refuse to pay and recover in days instead of weeks.

Denial of service: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack makes a service unavailable by overwhelming it with traffic or requests. A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack uses many machines at once, usually a botnet. Worked example: if 100,000 infected devices each send 2 megabits per second, total traffic is 100,000 x 2 = 200,000 megabits per second, or 200 gigabits per second, far more than a typical server link can carry. In 2016 the Mirai botnet, built from poorly secured cameras and routers with default passwords, launched huge attacks that disrupted major websites for many users. Default passwords on cheap devices became a crime tool.

Fraud, phishing and social engineering: Online fraud tricks people into giving money or information. Phishing uses fake emails, SMS or websites that look like a bank or service. Vishing uses phone calls. Social engineering in general exploits trust, fear or urgency rather than technical flaws. In Bangladesh, a very common pattern is a call or SMS pretending to be from a mobile financial service or a prize office: 'Your account will be blocked, tell me the code we just sent'. The code is actually the one-time password that lets the criminal take over the account. No genuine service asks for your PIN or OTP.

Phishing numbers, worked: Why do criminals send millions of messages? Because small rates add up. Suppose a criminal sends 10,000 fake messages, 3 percent of people click the link, and 10 percent of those enter their details. That is 10,000 x 0.03 = 300 clicks, and 300 x 0.10 = 30 victims. If each victim loses 5,000 taka, the criminal gains 150,000 taka from one cheap campaign. This is why awareness that lowers the click rate even a little prevents real harm.

Identity theft: Identity theft means using someone else's personal information, such as NID number, photos, phone number or bank details, to pretend to be them: opening accounts, taking loans, registering SIM cards, or committing crimes in their name. Leaked databases (lesson 13) feed this crime. Victims may spend months proving they did not take the loan.

Cyberbullying, harassment and image-based abuse: Using digital tools to threaten, stalk, humiliate or blackmail a person is a serious harm and often a crime. Examples: fake profiles made to insult someone, repeated threatening messages, sharing private photos without consent, or threatening to share them for money or favours, sometimes called sextortion. Victims are often young people and women. In Bangladesh, police run dedicated cyber support services, and victims can report to police cyber units and national helplines. The main advice: do not pay or negotiate, save evidence, report quickly.

Child sexual abuse material: Creating, possessing or sharing sexual images of children is a grave crime almost everywhere, and platforms use automated tools to detect known material. This is one area of cyber law with very wide international agreement.

Who the criminals are: Security people traditionally describe hackers by 'hats'. White hats are ethical hackers who test systems with permission (lesson 21). Black hats break in for personal gain or harm. Grey hats break in without permission but without clear criminal intent, often reporting the flaw afterwards; this is still usually illegal. Other groups: script kiddies who use ready-made tools without deep skill; hacktivists who attack for political causes; insiders, employees who misuse access, often the hardest to detect; organised crime groups running fraud and ransomware as businesses; and state-sponsored groups carrying out espionage or sabotage.

Why people commit cybercrime: Motives include money, revenge, curiosity, thrill, ideology, recognition among peers and, for states, intelligence and strategic advantage. Criminologists note that the distance between attacker and victim makes the harm feel less real to the attacker, and the belief that they will not be caught lowers the perceived risk. Good law enforcement and international cooperation (lesson 17) try to raise that risk.

Case 1, the Morris worm: On 2 November 1988, Robert Tappan Morris, a graduate student at Cornell University, released a self-spreading program onto the early internet, he said to measure its size. A bug made it reinfect machines repeatedly, slowing thousands of computers, an estimated several thousand, a large share of the internet at the time. He became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, receiving probation, community service and a fine. The case showed that 'just an experiment' can cause massive harm, and it led to the creation of the first computer emergency response team.

Case 2, WannaCry: On 12 May 2017, the WannaCry ransomware spread worldwide using a Windows vulnerability for which a patch had been released two months earlier. It infected hundreds of thousands of computers in about 150 countries, including many in the UK's National Health Service, where some appointments and operations were cancelled. A security researcher slowed it by registering a domain name the malware checked, acting as a kill switch. Lesson: patching quickly is an ethical duty for anyone running systems people depend on.

Case 3, the Bangladesh Bank heist: In February 2016, attackers who had gained access to Bangladesh Bank's systems used the international SWIFT messaging network to send fraudulent payment instructions to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, requesting transfers of nearly 1 billion US dollars from the bank's account. Most were blocked, but about 101 million dollars was transferred: about 20 million to Sri Lanka, which was recovered, partly after a spelling error in a recipient's name raised suspicion, and about 81 million to the Philippines, where much of it was laundered through casinos. The case showed that national institutions are targets, that insider-level access and weak internal controls are dangerous, and that cross-border crime is hard to recover from.

Real-life example 1, a student's 'prank': A university student uses a leaked password list to log into classmates' social media accounts and posts jokes. He thinks it is harmless fun. Legally it is unauthorised access, possibly identity misuse and harassment. Ethically it violates privacy and trust. Possible results: criminal complaint, expulsion and a permanent record. Many cyber crime cases involving young people start as 'pranks'.

Real-life example 2, the OTP call: A shopkeeper in Mirpur receives a call: 'I am calling from your mobile wallet's head office. Someone sent you 8,000 taka by mistake; we have sent you a code, please read it to me so we can reverse it.' Step by step, here is what is really happening. The criminal already has the shopkeeper's phone number, perhaps from a leaked list. He starts a 'forgot PIN' or login on the wallet app, which sends an OTP to the shopkeeper. The urgency and the authority of a 'head office' push the shopkeeper to read the code aloud. With it, the criminal resets access and empties the account within minutes. Every step is a crime: impersonation, fraud and unauthorised access. The defence is simple and must be repeated often: never share a PIN or OTP with anyone, and call the official helpline number yourself if unsure.

Common mistakes and exam points: 'If I don't damage anything, accessing without permission is legal.' No, access itself is usually the offence. 'Grey hat hacking is legal if I report the bug.' Usually still illegal without permission. 'Only experts commit cybercrime.' Script kiddies and social engineers need little skill. Exams ask: 'Classify computer crimes with examples', 'Explain types of malware', 'What is phishing and social engineering?', 'Describe the Bangladesh Bank heist', 'Discuss hacker categories and motives'.

Recap: Cybercrime covers crimes against computers (unauthorised access, malware, ransomware, DoS), crimes using computers (fraud, phishing, identity theft) and content crimes (harassment, image abuse, child abuse material). Small rates times huge volume make phishing profitable. Criminals range from script kiddies to insiders, organised gangs and states, driven by money, ideology, revenge or thrill. The Morris worm, WannaCry and the Bangladesh Bank heist show harm at scale. Next lesson explains how the law answers: cyber law foundations.
key_points: Cybercrime: crimes against computers, crimes using computers, and content-related crimes, with IP crimes often added.
Unauthorised access is usually an offence by itself, even without damage.
Malware types: virus, worm, trojan, spyware, keylogger, ransomware, botnet; ransomware now often adds data theft (double extortion).
DDoS overwhelms services using many machines; 100,000 bots x 2 Mbps = 200 Gbps.
Phishing and social engineering exploit trust and urgency; no genuine service asks for your PIN or OTP.
Criminal types: black, white and grey hats, script kiddies, hacktivists, insiders, organised crime and state actors.
Famous cases: Morris worm (1988), WannaCry (2017), Bangladesh Bank heist (2016, about 101 million dollars transferred, 81 million lost via the Philippines).
lessons.tip: For each type of cybercrime, remember one concrete example and one defence. That pair is the backbone of most exam answers and of real-life safety advice.

quiz.explain: 10,000 x 0.03 = 300 clicks, and 300 x 0.10 = 30 victims.

quiz.explain: Attackers sent fraudulent SWIFT messages to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

options: Grey hat, and still usually illegal

Users downloaded it from app stores

lessons.title: Cyber Law Foundations: Offences, Jurisdiction and International Cooperation
lessons.content:
Imagine a thief in country A uses a server in country B to steal money from a bank in country C, and sends it to an account in country D. Which police force investigates? Which court tries him? Which law even applies? Old criminal law was built for a world where the thief, the victim and the stolen goods were usually in the same town. Cyber law is the effort to update that world. This lesson covers why special computer crime laws were needed, the key laws and treaties that shaped them, how jurisdiction works online, and the rules about when platforms are responsible for what users post. The next two lessons apply these ideas to Bangladesh.

Why old laws were not enough: Traditional theft law usually requires taking someone's property so they no longer have it. But copying data leaves the original in place. Traditional trespass law is about entering physical land or buildings, not logging into a server. Forgery law was written for paper documents and signatures. In the 1980s, courts in several countries struggled with cases where hackers clearly did wrong, but no existing offence fitted neatly. Because criminal law follows the principle of legality, often expressed as 'no crime without a law', nobody can be punished for an act that the law does not clearly define as an offence. So lawmakers had to write new, specific offences.

The two parts of a crime: Criminal law usually needs two elements. The actus reus, the guilty act, such as accessing a computer without authorisation. And the mens rea, the guilty mind, such as knowing that you are not authorised, or intending to cause damage. This matters in cyber cases: an employee who accidentally opens a misconfigured folder lacks the guilty mind that a deliberate intruder has. Good cyber laws state clearly what act and what intention make an offence.

The UK Computer Misuse Act 1990: The UK's law was prompted partly by a 1980s case in which two men accessed a national information service using a password they had seen; they were prosecuted under a forgery law, and their convictions were eventually overturned because that law did not fit. The Computer Misuse Act created clear offences. Section 1: unauthorised access to computer material. Section 2: unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences. Section 3: unauthorised acts that impair the operation of a computer, covering malware and denial of service. A later amendment added an offence of making, supplying or obtaining articles, meaning tools, for use in these offences. Many Commonwealth countries borrowed from this structure.

The US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act: The United States passed the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) in 1986 and has amended it many times. It covers accessing a computer 'without authorization' or 'exceeding authorized access', and related acts like damaging protected computers and trafficking passwords. Critics argued the phrase 'exceeds authorized access' was so broad that breaking a website's terms of service could become a crime. In 2021, in Van Buren v. United States, the US Supreme Court read it more narrowly: it covers entering parts of a system you are not allowed to enter, not misusing information from areas you are allowed to access. The debate shows how vague words in cyber law can criminalise ordinary behaviour.

Other national laws: India's Information Technology Act 2000 gave legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures and created cyber offences. Its Section 66A, which punished sending 'offensive' or 'annoying' messages, was struck down by India's Supreme Court in 2015 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India because it was too vague and restricted free speech. This is a useful comparison for Bangladesh's own debates over speech offences in cyber laws (lessons 18 and 19). Malaysia, Singapore, Pakistan and many others have their own computer crime laws following similar patterns.

The Budapest Convention: The Council of Europe's Convention on Cybercrime, opened for signature in Budapest in November 2001 and in force since 2004, was the first international treaty on cybercrime. Many countries outside Europe have also joined. It does three things. First, it asks countries to create common offences: illegal access, illegal interception, data interference, system interference, misuse of devices, computer-related forgery and fraud, child sexual abuse material, and copyright infringement on a commercial scale. Second, it gives procedural powers: quick preservation of stored data, production orders, search and seizure of computer data, and interception under legal safeguards. Third, it sets up international cooperation, including a 24/7 network of contact points for urgent help.

A new UN treaty: In December 2024 the United Nations General Assembly adopted a new UN convention against cybercrime, after years of negotiation. Supporters see it as a way to include more countries in cooperation. Human rights groups and some technology companies worried that its broad wording could be used to target journalists, activists and security researchers. Its signing and ratification are ongoing, so check its current status. The debate echoes a theme of this whole course: cyber laws must stop real crime without becoming tools against legitimate speech and research.

Jurisdiction, who has power: Jurisdiction means a state's authority to make, apply and enforce law over a person or event. Several principles let a country claim jurisdiction. Territorial: the crime, or part of it, happened on its territory, for example the victim's server is there or the effects are felt there. Nationality: the offender is its citizen, even abroad. Passive personality: the victim is its citizen. Protective: the act threatens its national security or vital interests. Universal: for a few very grave crimes, any country may act. In cyber cases, several countries may claim jurisdiction at once, or none may be able to act effectively.

Worked jurisdiction example: A student in Khulna runs a phishing site hosted in Germany that targets customers of a bank in Malaysia, and the money is withdrawn in Dubai. Bangladesh can claim jurisdiction because the offender is a Bangladeshi citizen acting from Bangladesh (territorial and nationality). Malaysia can claim it because the victims and the bank are there (territorial effects and passive personality). Germany may act because the server is there. The United Arab Emirates may investigate the money withdrawal. In practice, the countries must cooperate: Germany can take down the site, Malaysia can share victim evidence, and Bangladesh can arrest and prosecute.

Cross-border evidence and MLATs: Evidence in cyber cases often sits on servers abroad, controlled by foreign companies. Traditionally, police request it through a mutual legal assistance treaty (MLAT): a formal government-to-government request, reviewed under the other country's law. MLATs protect rights but are slow, often taking months, while digital evidence can vanish in days. Newer approaches include direct requests to service providers under agreed rules, expedited preservation requests that freeze data while formal requests are prepared, and police-to-police networks. Extradition, sending a suspect to another country for trial, is also slow and depends on treaties and on the act being a crime in both countries, called dual criminality.

Intermediary liability: An intermediary is a service that carries or hosts other people's content: internet providers, hosting companies, social networks, marketplaces, search engines. Should Facebook be liable if a user posts defamation? Laws give different answers. In the United States, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 largely protects online platforms from being treated as the publisher of users' content. The European Union's e-Commerce Directive of 2000 created 'safe harbours': hosts are not liable if they do not know about illegal content and act quickly to remove it once notified. The EU's Digital Services Act, adopted in 2022, keeps that idea but adds duties such as transparency reports and risk assessments for very large platforms. Many countries, including Bangladesh, rely on notice-and-takedown requests to platforms through regulators.

Why intermediary rules matter: If platforms were fully liable for everything users post, they would censor heavily or shut down user content altogether. If they had no duties at all, illegal content could spread unchecked. Most systems try a middle path: protection from liability for content they do not know about, combined with a duty to act on valid notices. As a developer of any app with user content, even a small Bangla forum, you need a clear process for complaints and takedowns.

Good cyber law, a checklist: Legal scholars often judge cyber laws by a few tests. Clarity: can an ordinary person tell in advance what is forbidden? Intent: does the offence require a guilty mind, so honest mistakes are not crimes? Proportionality: are punishments matched to harm, so that peeking at a file is not treated like destroying a hospital system? Safeguards: do searches, interception and data demands need a judge's approval or similar oversight? Room for research: are good-faith security researchers protected when they test with care and report responsibly (lesson 21)? Free expression: are speech offences narrow and clearly defined? A law that fails these tests can harm the very citizens it claims to protect.

Real-life example 1, the DDoS-for-hire site: Teenagers in several countries pay small fees to 'booter' websites to knock gaming rivals offline. Police in different countries coordinate to seize the booter site's servers, identify customers from its records, and send warning letters or prosecute. Customers who thought it was a game discover that buying a DDoS attack is itself an offence in many laws.

Real-life example 2, the hosting company's notice: A small Bangladeshi web hosting company receives a notice that one customer's site sells fake exam question papers. If the company acts quickly, checks the notice, removes the illegal material and preserves records for police, it behaves responsibly and reduces its own legal risk. If it ignores repeated notices, it may face liability and regulatory action. A written takedown policy turns this into routine work.

Common mistakes and exam points: 'Cybercrime has no jurisdiction because the internet has no borders.' Countries use territorial, nationality and other principles, often overlapping. 'Platforms are always responsible for user posts.' Many laws protect them unless they know and fail to act. 'Vague cyber laws are harmless.' Vagueness can criminalise speech, as India's Section 66A case showed. Exams ask: 'Why were special computer crime laws needed?', 'Describe the offences in the Computer Misuse Act', 'Explain the Budapest Convention', 'Discuss jurisdiction principles with a cyber example', 'What is intermediary liability?'

Recap: Old laws on theft, trespass and forgery did not fit digital acts, and the principle of legality requires clear offences. Crimes need a guilty act and a guilty mind. The UK Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the US CFAA 1986 created core offences; vague wording, like India's struck-down Section 66A, threatens free speech. The Budapest Convention (2001) harmonises offences, procedures and cooperation, and a newer UN convention was adopted in 2024. Jurisdiction can be territorial, nationality, passive personality, protective or universal; MLATs and extradition are slow. Intermediary rules balance platform protection with takedown duties. Next we look closely at Bangladesh's ICT Act 2006.
key_points: Traditional theft, trespass and forgery laws did not fit digital acts; the principle of legality requires clearly defined offences.
Crimes usually need a guilty act (actus reus) and a guilty mind (mens rea).
UK Computer Misuse Act 1990: unauthorised access, access with intent to commit further offences, unauthorised acts impairing computers, and supplying tools.
US CFAA (1986) covers access without or exceeding authorisation; Van Buren (2021) narrowed 'exceeds authorized access'.
The Budapest Convention (2001) harmonises offences, gives procedural powers like data preservation, and builds a 24/7 cooperation network.
Jurisdiction principles: territorial, nationality, passive personality, protective, universal; MLATs and extradition are slow and need cooperation.
Intermediary liability rules (US Section 230, EU safe harbours and Digital Services Act) protect platforms but expect action on valid notices.
lessons.tip: For any cyber law question, structure your answer as: the act, the intent, the law that defines it, who has jurisdiction, and how evidence is obtained. Five points, every time.

lessons.title: Bangladesh Cyber Law I: The ICT Act 2006 and Related Laws
lessons.content:
Before 2006, if two Bangladeshi companies signed a deal by email, a court might ask: 'Where is the signed paper?' A digital file had no clear legal standing, and there was no specific law punishing someone who broke into a computer. As banks, government offices and businesses moved online, Bangladesh needed rules that treated electronic records as real records and computer crimes as real crimes. The main answer was the Information and Communication Technology Act, 2006, usually called the ICT Act. This lesson explains what it did, the famous controversy around its Section 57, and the other laws a Bangladeshi computing professional should know. Laws change, and some parts described here were later replaced, so the lesson keeps to well-established points and you should always check the current text. This is general education, not legal advice.

Why the ICT Act was needed: Three problems pushed for it. First, e-commerce and e-government need legal certainty: a contract made online, a digitally signed tax return or an electronic land record must be valid in court. Second, there had to be trust infrastructure, meaning a system for issuing and checking digital signatures. Third, there were no clear offences for hacking, damaging computer systems or tampering with source code. Similar laws existed elsewhere, such as India's IT Act 2000, and the UN's model laws on electronic commerce and electronic signatures guided many countries.

What the Act covers, the big picture: The ICT Act does several things at once. It gives legal recognition to electronic records and electronic or digital signatures. It sets up a regulatory system for certifying authorities that issue digital signature certificates. It describes duties of subscribers who hold such certificates. It created a set of offences and penalties for computer-related wrongs. And it provided for special Cyber Tribunals to try those offences, along with investigation powers.

Legal recognition of electronic records: The Act says that where a law requires information to be in writing or in printed form, that requirement can be met by an electronic record, as long as it is accessible and usable for later reference. Similarly, where a law requires a signature, a digital signature made according to the Act can satisfy it. This is the foundation of e-government in Bangladesh: online forms, e-tender submissions, digital certificates and electronic filings all depend on this principle.

Digital signatures, a quick recap: You studied the technology in deep-cse-6-2. A digital signature uses public key cryptography. Step 1, the signer's software computes a hash of the document, a short fingerprint. Step 2, it encrypts that hash with the signer's private key; the result is the signature. Step 3, the receiver computes the hash of the received document, decrypts the signature with the signer's public key, and compares. If the two hashes match, the document is unchanged and was signed by the holder of that private key. Changing even one character of the document produces a completely different hash, so tampering is detected.

Certifying authorities and the CCA: A public key is only useful if you can trust whose key it is. That is the job of a certifying authority (CA): a trusted organisation that checks a person's or company's identity and issues a digital certificate binding their name to their public key. The ICT Act created the office of the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA), which licenses and supervises CAs in Bangladesh, sets standards, and maintains the root of trust. So the chain is: the CCA trusts licensed CAs, licensed CAs vouch for subscribers, and anyone can verify a subscriber's signature by checking that chain.

Duties of certificate holders: A subscriber, meaning someone who holds a digital signature certificate, must take reasonable care to keep the private key secret, and must ask the CA to revoke the certificate quickly if the key is compromised. This mirrors the duty you have with a bank PIN. If an employee leaves the private key on a shared office computer and someone signs a tender with it, questions of responsibility follow.

What this means for developers: If you build systems for Bangladeshi government offices, banks or businesses, the ICT Act's trust framework shapes your design. Systems that accept signed documents must verify signatures and certificate chains properly, check whether certificates have been revoked, and store signed files unchanged with their signatures. Audit logs should record who signed or changed what and when, with accurate time. Private keys used by servers must be protected, ideally in hardware security modules. A system that quietly accepts unsigned or invalid files undermines the legal value that the Act gives to electronic records.

The offences: The ICT Act listed a number of computer-related offences with punishments. They included, in broad terms, damaging computers or computer systems without permission, tampering with computer source code, hacking that destroys or alters information or reduces its value, and publishing certain kinds of content in electronic form. It also included offences linked to the digital signature system, such as misrepresentation to obtain a certificate and publishing false certificates. Several of these offence sections were later repealed and replaced by the Digital Security Act 2018 (lesson 19), while the parts on electronic records and digital signatures continued.

Section 57, the controversy: The most debated part of the ICT Act was Section 57. In broad terms, it made it an offence to publish or transmit in electronic form material that was fake or obscene, or that could tend to deprave or corrupt people, harm law and order, damage the image of the state or a person, or hurt religious sentiment. The 2013 amendment to the Act made offences under it, including Section 57, non-bailable and allowed arrest without a warrant, and raised the maximum prison term sharply, to 14 years. Journalists, bloggers, students and ordinary social media users were arrested under it for posts and comments.

Why Section 57 was criticised: Critics, including human rights organisations, lawyers and journalists, raised several points. The words were vague: 'tend to deprave', 'image of the state' and 'hurt religious sentiment' could cover almost any critical post, so nobody knew in advance what was forbidden, against the principle of legality (lesson 17). It mixed very different things in one section: obscenity, defamation, religious offence and public order. The punishments were seen as disproportionate for speech. And it created a chilling effect: people stopped posting legitimate criticism out of fear. Supporters argued that online rumours and hate content had triggered real violence and needed strong deterrence. The debate is similar to India's Section 66A, which India's Supreme Court struck down in 2015.

What happened next: Under domestic and international pressure, the government replaced Section 57 and several other offence sections when it passed the Digital Security Act in 2018. However, many critics said the new law carried similar vague speech offences into new sections. That story continues in lesson 19. The key lesson for engineers: how a law is worded matters as much as its purpose, because vague words give wide discretion to whoever enforces them.

Cyber Tribunal and investigation: The Act provided for special Cyber Tribunals to try cyber offences and set out who could investigate them. Specialised tribunals help because judges and prosecutors build expertise with digital evidence, which you will study in lesson 20. Courts also need to understand concepts like IP addresses, logs and hashes, which is why technical experts are often called as witnesses.

The Bangladesh Telecommunication Act 2001: This law created the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC), which licenses mobile operators and internet service providers, manages spectrum, and issues directions to operators. It also includes offences related to telecommunication misuse. In practice, BTRC is often the channel through which content takedown or blocking requests are sent to operators and platforms, so it matters for anyone running online services.

The Pornography Control Act 2012: This law criminalises producing, distributing and possessing pornography, including through electronic means, with specific and heavier provisions concerning children. It is also used in cases where intimate images are recorded or shared without consent, a form of image-based abuse discussed in lesson 16.

The Right to Information Act 2009: This law gives citizens the right to request information from public authorities, and created an Information Commission to hear complaints. It balances transparency against exemptions for things like security and personal privacy. For engineers in government projects, it means records systems should be built so that disclosable information can be found and released efficiently.

The Evidence Act and digital records: The Evidence Act of 1872 is the basic law about what can be used as proof in Bangladeshi courts. It was amended in 2022 to deal more directly with digital records as evidence. This connects law with the forensic practices in lesson 20: how digital evidence is collected and preserved affects whether a court will trust it.

Real-life example 1, an e-tender with a digital signature: A construction firm in Sylhet submits a government e-tender signed with a digital certificate issued by a licensed CA. Later a rival claims the bid was altered after submission. The procurement office verifies the signature: the hash of the stored bid matches the hash inside the signature, and the certificate chains to a licensed CA under the CCA. The bid is proven unaltered and authentic. This is the ICT Act's electronic-record framework working as intended.

Real-life example 2, a Facebook post case: A university student posts a sharply worded criticism of a local official. Under a vague speech offence, he could face arrest even if the post is opinion rather than a false statement of fact. Under a well-drafted law, defamation would be a civil or narrowly defined matter, with clear defences like truth and fair comment. The contrast shows why legal drafting is an ethical issue: the same post can mean a debate or a prison cell depending on a few words in a statute.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students write that the ICT Act was entirely repealed; its electronic records and digital signature framework continued, while several offence sections were replaced in 2018. Others mix up CCA (controller) and CA (issuer). Exams ask: 'What are the main objectives of the ICT Act 2006?', 'Explain the role of the Controller of Certifying Authorities', 'How do digital signatures provide legal validity?', 'Discuss Section 57 and its criticism', 'Name other Bangladeshi laws relevant to ICT'.

Recap: The ICT Act 2006 gave legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, created the Controller of Certifying Authorities to license certifying authorities, set duties for certificate holders, created computer offences and provided for Cyber Tribunals. Section 57, a broad speech offence made harsher in 2013, was heavily criticised for vagueness, disproportionate punishment and chilling effects, and was replaced along with other offence sections in 2018. Related laws include the Telecommunication Act 2001 (BTRC), the Pornography Control Act 2012, the Right to Information Act 2009 and the Evidence Act as amended for digital records. Next lesson follows the story from the Digital Security Act 2018 to the Cyber Security Act 2023 and after.
key_points: The ICT Act 2006 gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, the basis of e-government and e-commerce in Bangladesh.
The Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) licenses and supervises certifying authorities that issue digital signature certificates.
A digital signature encrypts the document's hash with a private key; verification compares hashes using the public key, so any change is detected.
Certificate holders must keep private keys secret and request revocation if compromised.
The Act created computer offences and Cyber Tribunals; several offence sections were later replaced by the Digital Security Act 2018.
Section 57, a broad speech offence made harsher in 2013 (non-bailable, maximum 14 years), was criticised for vagueness, disproportion and chilling effects.
Related laws: Telecommunication Act 2001 (BTRC), Pornography Control Act 2012, Right to Information Act 2009, Evidence Act (amended for digital records).
lessons.tip: Split the ICT Act into two halves in your notes: the 'trust' half (electronic records, digital signatures, CCA) which continued, and the 'offences' half, parts of which were replaced. Exam answers become much clearer.

options: Licensing and supervising certifying authorities that issue digital signature certificates
quiz.explain: The CCA is the root of trust that licenses and supervises CAs.

options: The hash computed from the received document matches the hash recovered from the signature
The file size is the same
The signer's name is typed at the bottom
quiz.explain: Any change produces a different hash, so matching hashes show integrity.

options: It was too narrow to cover any offence
It was vague and could punish legitimate speech, creating a chilling effect
quiz.explain: Words like 'image of the state' and 'hurt religious sentiment' were vague and broad.

quiz.explain: The Bangladesh Telecommunication Act 2001 established the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission.

options: Its electronic records and digital signature framework continued, while several offence sections were replaced
It was renamed the Pornography Control Act
It now only covers telecom licences
quiz.explain: The Digital Security Act 2018 replaced several offence sections, but the trust framework remained.

lessons.title: Bangladesh Cyber Law II: From the Digital Security Act to the Cyber Security Act and After
lessons.content:
Think of a city that keeps rebuilding the same bridge. Each new version is announced as stronger and safer, yet citizens keep asking whether the problems of the old bridge were really fixed or just painted over. Bangladesh's cyber security laws have had a similar story: the ICT Act's offences (2006), then the Digital Security Act (2018), then the Cyber Security Act (2023), then a further replacement after 2024. This lesson explains what these laws try to do, the kinds of offences they contain, why they were controversial, and how a Bangladeshi engineer or citizen can stay safe and report crime. Because these laws have changed several times and may change again, this lesson describes patterns and well-established facts, not section-by-section details. Always read the current official text before relying on any specific provision. This is education, not legal advice.

What a cyber security law tries to do: A national cyber security law typically has two sides. The protective side defends systems and people: it creates offences for hacking, malware, fraud and attacks on important infrastructure, sets up an agency and an incident response team, and gives investigators powers to collect digital evidence. The content side regulates what people publish online: false information, defamation, hate speech, religious offence and threats to public order. Most international criticism of Bangladesh's laws focused on the content side, while the protective side was widely seen as necessary.

The Digital Security Act 2018: In 2018 Bangladesh passed the Digital Security Act (DSA). It repealed Section 57 and several other offence sections of the ICT Act (lesson 18), while keeping the ICT Act's framework for electronic records and digital signatures. The DSA created a Digital Security Agency and a National Digital Security Council, introduced the idea of critical information infrastructure, and listed a wide range of offences, from illegal access and digital fraud to several speech-related offences.

Critical information infrastructure: An important and largely uncontroversial idea in these laws is critical information infrastructure (CII): computer systems whose disruption would seriously harm national security, the economy, public health or safety, such as power grids, banking networks, telecom networks and key government databases. Laws designate such systems and require their operators to follow security standards and report incidents, and they treat attacks on them more seriously. The Bangladesh Bank heist (lesson 16) shows why: financial infrastructure is a national target.

The main offence families: Across the DSA and its successor, offences fell into recognisable families. First, attacks on systems: illegal access to computers and especially to critical infrastructure, damaging data, spreading malware, and disrupting services. Second, fraud and identity crimes: digital or electronic fraud, identity fraud and impersonation, and collecting or using someone's identity information without lawful authority. Third, content offences: publishing false or offensive information, defamation, content said to hurt religious sentiment, content said to harm law and order, and certain content about national history and symbols. Fourth, related offences such as breaching official secrecy through digital means and assisting other offences.

Why the DSA was criticised: Journalists' organisations, human rights groups, lawyers, United Nations experts and foreign governments raised strong concerns. Many speech offences were vaguely worded, similar to the old Section 57. Some offences were non-bailable, and police had powers to search and arrest without a warrant in certain situations, which critics said invited abuse. Cases were filed against journalists, writers, students, cartoonists and ordinary social media users, often by people close to powerful figures. A widely reported case was that of writer Mushtaq Ahmed, who was arrested under the DSA and died in custody in February 2021, causing protests. Supporters argued the law was needed against rumours that had sparked communal violence and against real cyber crime. But the gap between the law's stated aims and its use against critics became the central issue.

The chilling effect, explained: A chilling effect happens when people avoid lawful speech because they fear punishment under a vague law. You do not need many arrests to create it; a few well-publicised cases are enough. Engineers can understand this like a system with a harsh, unpredictable penalty: rational users stop doing anything near the edge. The cost is invisible but real: fewer investigative stories, fewer whistleblowers, less honest public debate. This is why clarity and proportionality (lesson 17) are not technicalities but protections for democracy.

Balancing security and liberty, a simple test: How can a law fight real online harm without silencing people? Lawyers often use a three-part test drawn from international human rights law. First, legality: the restriction must be set out in a clear, accessible law. Second, legitimate aim: it must protect something recognised as important, such as other people's rights or reputation, national security, public order, public health or morals. Third, necessity and proportionality: it must be the least restrictive way to reach that aim, and the punishment must fit the harm. Apply it to a post that falsely claims a named shopkeeper sells poisoned food: there is a clear harm to a person, so a narrow defamation remedy can pass. Apply it to a post that simply criticises a government policy: there is no legitimate aim in punishing it, so a law that does would fail.

The Cyber Security Act 2023: In 2023, after continued criticism, Bangladesh replaced the DSA with the Cyber Security Act (CSA). The government presented it as a reform: some punishments were reduced, some offences were made bailable, and for defamation the punishment was changed to a fine rather than prison. The agency was renamed as a national cyber security agency. However, many critics said the CSA kept most of the DSA's structure and much of its vague speech-related wording, so the core risks remained. Cases already filed under the DSA raised questions about how they would continue.

After 2024: Following the political change of August 2024, the interim government moved to replace the Cyber Security Act 2023 again. In 2025 a new cyber security ordinance was issued, presented as removing several of the most criticised speech offences and focusing more on protecting systems and people from real cyber attacks and online harms. Because this process happened recently and may be followed by further legislation, review and court decisions, you must check the current law and its official text. The safest summary for an exam: Bangladesh's cyber law has moved from the ICT Act's offences, to the DSA 2018, to the CSA 2023, and then to a further replacement, with each change driven largely by the debate over speech offences.

Personal data in the newer laws: Another area that keeps growing is personal data. Cyber security laws in Bangladesh have included offences about collecting, selling or using someone's identity information, such as NID details, without lawful authority, and the country has worked on a separate personal data protection law (lesson 14). For developers this means that the leaked customer lists and NID databases sometimes offered for sale online are not just unethical to use; touching them can be a crime. Build systems that collect the minimum data, protect it well and log access.

What stays constant across versions: Despite the changes, some things remain stable and are worth learning well. Unauthorised access, malware, damaging data, digital fraud, identity theft and attacks on critical infrastructure are crimes in every version and in almost every country. Online sexual harassment, blackmail and non-consensual sharing of intimate images are treated seriously, often under multiple laws. Investigators can, with proper authority, seize devices and request data from service providers. And the ICT Act's framework for electronic records and digital signatures continues to support e-government and e-commerce.

Incident response: Bangladesh has a government computer incident response team (often known as BGD e-GOV CIRT) that monitors threats, issues alerts and helps government and critical infrastructure organisations respond to incidents. Banks and financial institutions also follow Bangladesh Bank's information security guidelines. For engineers, this means that in a serious incident at a critical organisation, you may need to report to these bodies, preserve evidence and follow their guidance.

How to report cyber crime in Bangladesh: Practical steps that remain useful whatever the current law: Step 1, stay calm and do not negotiate with blackmailers or pay them. Step 2, preserve evidence: take screenshots showing usernames, profile links, dates and times; save message links; do not delete the conversation. Step 3, secure your accounts: change passwords, enable two-step verification, log out of unknown devices. Step 4, report to the platform using its reporting tools. Step 5, report to police: the national emergency number 999 can direct you, police have dedicated cyber crime units, and Bangladesh Police has run a cyber support service for women. For financial fraud, also call your bank or mobile wallet's official helpline immediately to block transactions.

As an engineer, staying on the right side: Some professional habits keep you safe under any version of the law. Test only systems you own or have written permission to test (lesson 21). Never use leaked data, even for 'research'. Keep logs and evidence when your system is attacked, and report through proper channels. When you post opinions, criticise ideas and actions with facts rather than making false factual claims about people. And when you build platforms, have clear terms, a complaint and takedown process, and a policy for responding to lawful government requests that protects users' rights.

Real-life example 1, a bank's DDoS incident: A Bangladeshi bank's website is hit by a DDoS attack during salary week. The bank's security team activates its incident plan: filters traffic through its provider, informs Bangladesh Bank and the relevant CIRT as its rules require, preserves logs, and files a complaint with police. Investigators later trace the botnet's controller with help from foreign partners (lesson 17). This is the protective side of cyber law working as intended.

Real-life example 2, a satirical cartoon: An artist posts a satirical cartoon about a policy. Under a vaguely worded speech offence, someone files a complaint claiming it harms 'public order', and the artist is detained. Under a narrowly drafted law that protects opinion and satire and requires proof of real incitement to violence, the complaint would fail. The same drawing, two very different outcomes: this is the heart of the debate that drove Bangladesh's repeated legal reforms.

Common mistakes and exam points: Students write outdated section numbers as if still current; it is better to name the law, the year and the type of offence, and say 'under the law in force at the time'. Others treat all cyber laws as purely about hacking, missing the content side, or describe them as purely about speech, missing real crime protection. Exams ask: 'Trace the development of cyber laws in Bangladesh', 'What were the main criticisms of the Digital Security Act?', 'What changes did the Cyber Security Act 2023 bring?', 'Explain critical information infrastructure', 'How should a victim report cyber crime in Bangladesh?'

Recap: Bangladesh's cyber law moved from ICT Act offences (2006) to the Digital Security Act (2018), the Cyber Security Act (2023), and a further replacement after 2024. These laws protect systems and people (illegal access, malware, fraud, identity crimes, critical infrastructure) and also regulate content, which drew strong criticism for vagueness, harsh penalties, arrest powers and chilling effects, including well-known cases against writers and journalists. Core crimes stay constant; speech provisions keep changing, so always check the current text. Report crime by preserving evidence, securing accounts and contacting platforms, banks and police. Next lesson explains how digital evidence is collected and kept trustworthy: digital forensics.

quiz.explain: CII covers systems vital to national security, economy, health or safety, so attacks on them are treated seriously.

Do not pay, preserve evidence, secure accounts and report to the platform and police
