quiz.q: A hiring model trained on ten years of mostly male hires starts preferring men. This is mainly...
quiz.explain: The data reflects past discrimination, which the model learns and repeats.

quiz.q: Group A selection rate is 0.30 and group B is 0.15. What is the ratio, and does it pass the four-fifths rule?
quiz.explain: 0.15 / 0.30 = 0.5, which is below 0.8, so it signals possible adverse impact.

quiz.q: Equal opportunity as a fairness measure compares...
options: The colour of the user interface
True positive rates among qualified people in each group
quiz.explain: It asks whether equally qualified people have the same chance of being selected.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, social scoring by public authorities is classified as...
quiz.explain: Social scoring by public authorities is among the prohibited practices.

quiz.q: Why does deleting the 'gender' column not guarantee a fair model?
options: Because other features can act as proxies for gender
Because gender is always needed for accuracy
Because the law requires gender data
quiz.explain: Features like hobbies, names or phone usage can correlate with gender and carry the same bias.

lessons.title: Computing and Society: Social Impact and a Capstone Ethics Case
lessons.content:
A village girl in Kurigram attends an online class on her mother's phone, while a classmate in Gulshan joins from a laptop with fast broadband. An old rickshaw puller loses customers to a ride-sharing app he cannot use. A child in Old Dhaka breaks open discarded circuit boards to sell the copper, breathing fumes all day. None of them wrote a line of code, yet all of them live with the results of decisions made by computing professionals. This final lesson steps back to look at computing's wider effects on society: the digital divide, automation and work, environmental impact and e-waste, and accessibility. Then we bring the whole course together in one worked capstone case, a health app for Dhaka, using the decision method from lesson 4. You will finish with a personal checklist you can carry into your career.

Why social impact belongs in an engineering course: Technology is not neutral in its effects. The same app can empower some people and exclude others. Professional codes (lesson 6) ask engineers to consider the public good, not just the client's wishes. And many failures in this course, from biased algorithms to data leaks, happened because nobody asked early enough: who else is affected?

The digital divide: The digital divide is the gap between people who have effective access to digital technology and those who do not. It has several layers. Access: whether you have a device, electricity and an affordable internet connection. Skills: whether you can use digital tools safely and well. Use and outcomes: whether access actually improves your education, income and health. Gaps often follow lines of income, rural versus urban, gender, age, disability and language. During COVID-19 school closures, many students in Bangladesh and around the world could not join online classes because they lacked devices or data, so learning losses widened existing inequality.

How engineers can narrow the divide: Design for low-cost Android phones, small screens and slow, expensive data. Make apps work offline and sync later. Keep app size small. Provide Bangla interfaces and voice options for people who read less comfortably. Test with rural users, older users and women, not just with classmates in Dhaka. Bangladesh's own services, such as union digital centres that help citizens access government services, show how intermediaries and local presence can bridge gaps that technology alone cannot.

Automation and work: Computing automates tasks: bank tellers are replaced by ATMs and apps, data entry by software, and some factory jobs by machines. New jobs also appear: app developers, delivery riders, digital marketers, freelancers. Bangladesh has a large community of online freelancers working for clients around the world. Economists generally find that automation changes which tasks people do more than it simply removes all work, but the transition can be painful for people whose skills lose value, and benefits may flow mainly to owners and the highly skilled. In Bangladesh's garment industry, a major employer of women, increased automation raises questions about retraining and fair transition.

The gig economy: Platforms for ride-sharing, food delivery and freelancing offer flexible work, but workers are often classified as independent contractors without sick pay, insurance or job security, and algorithms decide their pay, ratings and access to jobs. Ethical issues include transparency about how pay is calculated, fair processes when accounts are suspended, safety for riders, and whether workers can raise complaints to a human. Engineers who design these algorithms are shaping working conditions for thousands of people.

Environmental impact: Computing uses energy and materials. Data centres consume large amounts of electricity and water for cooling; training very large AI models uses significant energy. Devices require mining of metals, often under poor conditions. Engineers can reduce impact by writing efficient code, avoiding needless computation, choosing efficient hosting, designing devices that last longer, and supporting repair rather than replacement. Efficiency is not only good engineering; it is also an ethical responsibility.

E-waste, worked numbers: Electronic waste includes discarded phones, computers, chargers and appliances. The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 reported that the world generated about 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, and only about 22.3 percent was documented as properly collected and recycled. That means roughly 62 x 0.223, about 13.8 million tonnes, were formally recycled, leaving most of it unaccounted for. Spread over about 8 billion people, 62 million tonnes is 62,000,000,000 kg / 8,000,000,000, about 7.75 kg per person per year. In Bangladesh, much e-waste is handled informally, sometimes by children, who burn cables and break boards without protection, exposing themselves to lead, mercury and other toxins. Bangladesh has issued rules on hazardous e-waste management; check the current rules.

What responsible e-waste practice looks like: Buy durable devices and keep them longer. Repair when possible. Erase personal data properly before disposal (lesson 15). Give old devices to authorised collectors or take-back programmes rather than the cheapest scrap buyer. Companies can design for disassembly, offer take-back schemes, and avoid planned obsolescence, the practice of designing products to become useless sooner than necessary.

Accessibility: Accessibility means designing technology that people with disabilities can use: people who are blind or have low vision, deaf or hard of hearing, have motor impairments, or have cognitive or learning differences. The World Health Organization estimates that about 1.3 billion people, around 16 percent of the world's population, experience significant disability. For an app with 500,000 users, 16 percent is 500,000 x 0.16 = 80,000 people who may need accessible design. Bangladesh's Persons with Disabilities Rights and Protection Act 2013 recognises the rights of persons with disabilities, including access to information and communication.

How to build accessible software: Follow the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), which organise requirements under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. In practice: add text descriptions to images for screen readers, ensure enough colour contrast, never rely on colour alone, make every action possible with a keyboard or assistive switch, label form fields clearly, provide captions for videos, avoid flashing content, keep language simple, and test with real assistive technology such as screen readers on Android and iOS, including in Bangla. Accessible design often helps everyone: captions help people in noisy buses, and clear layouts help older users.

Capstone case, the Dhaka health app: Now let us use everything from this course. A startup asks you to build 'ShasthoSheba', an app that lets Dhaka residents book doctor appointments, store medical records, and get AI symptom suggestions. The investors want fast growth and data-driven advertising. Apply the decision method from lesson 4. Step 1, facts: the app handles sensitive health data; users include low-income and older people; the AI may be wrong; advertising could target sick people. Step 2, stakeholders: patients, doctors, the startup, investors, families, regulators and people who cannot use smartphones.

Capstone, analysing the options: Option A: collect as much data as possible, sell targeted ads to pharmaceutical companies, launch quickly with an English-only interface. Option B: collect only what is needed, encrypt records, no health-based advertising, Bangla interface and accessibility from day one, AI suggestions clearly labelled as not a diagnosis with a doctor in the loop, launch slightly later. A utilitarian view (lesson 2) asks which option gives more total benefit with less harm; Option A risks massive harm from leaks and misleading AI. A rights view (lesson 3) says patients' privacy and dignity are not for sale. Virtue ethics asks what an honest, caring engineer would do. Law agrees: privacy and data protection principles (lessons 13 to 15), consumer protection (lesson 22), and AI accountability (lesson 24) all favour Option B.

Capstone, the decision and how to argue for it: Recommend Option B, and present it in business terms too: trust is the main asset of a health app, a data breach could destroy the company, and accessible Bangla design expands the market. Document the decision, the risks you raised and the safeguards built in. If management insists on harmful practices, use internal escalation, follow your professional code, and if the public is at serious risk, consider the whistleblowing guidance from lesson 7. Plan forensic readiness and incident response (lessons 19 and 20), and commission a penetration test before launch (lesson 21).

Real-life example 1, the offline-first school app: A team of students in Rangpur builds a homework app for local schools. Instead of assuming fast internet, they make lessons downloadable when a connection is available, use small Bangla audio files, and design large buttons for cheap phones. Usage among rural students jumps compared with an earlier online-only version. Thinking about the digital divide turned a good idea into a useful product.

Real-life example 2, the old laptops: A software company in Chattogram upgrades 100 laptops. Instead of selling them to a scrap dealer, it securely wipes them, donates working ones to a local school with basic training, and sends broken ones to an authorised recycler. The cost is small, the school gains computers, no customer data leaks, and no child burns the cables in an alley. Ethical choices often look like this: ordinary, practical and planned.

Your personal ethics checklist: Before you build or ship anything, ask: Is it legal, and is it honest? Who could be harmed, including people who are not my users? What data do I collect, and do I really need it? Is it secure enough for the harm a breach would cause? Is it fair to different groups, and accessible to people with disabilities and limited connectivity? Would I be comfortable explaining this decision to the people affected, or seeing it in the news? Who is accountable, and how can users complain? If any answer worries you, slow down and raise it.

Common mistakes and exam points: 'Social impact is someone else's job.' Engineers' design choices create much of it. 'Accessibility is only for a few users.' About 16 percent of people have significant disability, and accessible design helps many more. 'Throwing away old electronics is harmless.' Most e-waste is not properly recycled. Exams ask: 'Explain the digital divide and how to reduce it', 'Discuss the social impact of automation', 'What is e-waste and why is it a problem in Bangladesh?', 'Describe accessibility principles for software', 'Analyse an ethical dilemma using a structured method'.

Recap and what next: The digital divide has access, skills and outcome layers; offline-first, low-data, Bangla and accessible design narrow it. Automation and the gig economy change work and demand fair algorithms. Computing's environmental cost includes energy and e-waste: about 62 million tonnes in 2022, only about 22.3 percent formally recycled, about 7.75 kg per person. Accessibility, guided by WCAG, serves about 16 percent of people directly. The capstone showed how ethics, privacy, security, law and AI fairness combine into one decision. Across 25 lessons you have studied ethical theories, professional codes, intellectual property, privacy, cyber crime, Bangladeshi and international cyber law, forensics, ethical hacking, e-commerce, free speech, AI ethics and social impact. Carry these ideas into Software Engineering (deep-cse-6-8), Machine Learning (deep-cse-6-11), and every project you build: good engineers ask not only 'can we build it?' but 'should we, and for whom?'
key_points: The digital divide has layers of access, skills and outcomes, often following income, location, gender, age, disability and language.
Engineers narrow it with low-cost, offline-first, low-data, Bangla and accessible design tested with diverse users.
Automation and the gig economy change work; algorithm designers shape pay, ratings and fairness for workers.
About 62 million tonnes of e-waste were generated in 2022, only about 22.3% formally recycled, about 7.75 kg per person.
Accessibility follows WCAG's four principles (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust); about 16% of people have significant disability.
The capstone health app case combines ethical theories, privacy, security, consumer law and AI fairness into one structured decision.
A personal checklist: legal and honest, who is harmed, minimal data, secure, fair, accessible, explainable, accountable.
lessons.tip: For any ethics essay, end with a concrete recommendation and its safeguards, and explain it in terms the business understands as well as in ethical terms. Examiners and managers both reward answers that are principled and practical.
lessons.task: Choose an app idea you would like to build. Write a one-page ethics plan using the personal checklist: stakeholders, data collected and why, security measures, fairness and accessibility checks, and how users can complain.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the layers of the digital divide?
options: Choice of programming language by developers
Whether use improves outcomes like income and education
quiz.explain: The divide is about access, skills and outcomes for users, not developers' language choices.

quiz.q: If 62 million tonnes of e-waste are shared among about 8 billion people, how much is it per person?
Which four principles organise the WCAG accessibility guidelines?
quiz.explain: WCAG groups its requirements under perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.

quiz.q: An app has 500,000 users. About how many might have a significant disability, using the WHO estimate of 16%?
In the capstone health app, why is Option B the better recommendation?
options: It protects sensitive data, avoids exploiting patients, is accessible, and keeps doctors in the loop for AI
It earns the most from advertising
It uses only English to reduce cost
quiz.explain: Ethical theories, privacy law, consumer protection and AI accountability all support Option B's safeguards.
